section: Company by Company — How Each Giant Runs Its Storage
hook: Every giant's storage stack looks different. Four questions decode any of them. Which four?
title: Four questions decode any company's storage stack
body: Google, Meta, AWS and Netflix all run storage at enormous scale, yet their stacks look nothing alike. Listing their systems tells you little. Four questions tell you why. What did they **build vs buy**? How big is it, using only numbers they published, with the year? How do they scale it and migrate it? And what is their **philosophy**: cloud or on-prem, one standard system or many specialised ones?
takeaway: Components tell you what a company runs. Philosophy tells you why.
deeper:
**Turn the view sideways:** Storage is usually taught one layer at a time: file systems, object stores, databases, caches, lakes. Here you look at one company across every layer instead, so you see the shape of the whole stack and the reasons behind it.

**Why each question matters:** Build vs buy shows where a company thinks its advantage lies. Published scale, always tied to a year, keeps comparisons honest. Migrations show how a company changes a live system without breaking it, the hardest skill in storage. Philosophy explains why two companies with similar workloads end up with very different stacks.

**Internals stay black boxes:** Names like Colossus, Tectonic or Dynamo appear without re-teaching their mechanics. The point is where each system sits and why it exists.

**Use it at work:** The same four questions apply to your own organisation. Answer them honestly and you have a one-page map of your storage and the reasons behind it.

quiz.q: Two companies both run huge key-value workloads. One built its own store; the other uses a managed service. Which question explains the difference, and what would you check?
quiz.a: Build vs buy, read through philosophy. Check whether storage is their product or their biggest cost. If so, building pays; if not, they buy and build only thin layers.

mcq.q: Which of the four questions covers "one standard system vs many specialised systems"?
options: Philosophy
Published scale
What they built and bought
How they migrate
mcq.why: Philosophy covers standardize vs polyglot, alongside build vs buy and cloud vs on-prem as a company's guiding choices.

section: Company by Company — How Each Giant Runs Its Storage
hook: Apple runs iCloud for hundreds of millions of users. Its storage story fits in one paragraph. Why?
title: Apple publishes almost nothing, so its section is tiny
body: What you can know about a company's storage depends on what it publishes, and companies publish **unevenly**. Google and Meta publish research papers. AWS publishes product pages and re:Invent talks. Netflix, Uber and LinkedIn publish engineering blogs. Apple publishes almost nothing. So Apple's section is short because the evidence is thin, not because its storage is small. When a fact is not published, the honest move is to say so instead of guessing.
takeaway: Silence in the sources is not a small system. Write "not published".
deeper:
**Different channels, different detail:** A research paper gives mechanisms and measured numbers, like Tectonic's 1,590 PB cluster. A product page gives headline totals, like S3's 700 trillion objects. A blog gives design detail but often no totals: Netflix has no verified total for its warehouse or Cassandra fleet in these sources.

**What Apple did make public:** Two things. The FoundationDB Record Layer paper (2019) says CloudKit hosts billions of logical databases on FoundationDB. And Advanced Data Protection (2022) lets users end-to-end encrypt most iCloud data.

**The discipline:** No published storage compliance design exists here for Uber, Netflix or LinkedIn, so none is described. Inventing one to fill a table cell is how wrong facts spread through design docs and interviews.

**Apply it:** In a design review, tag each claim as published, measured by you, or assumed. Assumptions are fine. Hidden assumptions are not.

quiz.q: A colleague's slide says Netflix stores "about 100 PB in Cassandra" and cites nothing. How should you treat it?
quiz.a: As unverified. Netflix publishes design detail more than totals, and no verified Cassandra total exists in these sources. Ask for the source and year, or label it an estimate.

mcq.q: Why is Apple's storage section much shorter than Google's?
options: Apple publishes almost nothing about its infrastructure
Apple runs far less storage than Google does
Apple buys all of its storage from AWS
Apple's storage systems are too new to describe
mcq.why: Coverage follows publication. Google and Meta publish papers; Apple publishes almost nothing, so less can be stated honestly.

section: How to read the stack diagrams
hook: Every storage stack, from Google to Dropbox, fits the same six shelves. Which data goes on which shelf?
title: Six layers fit every company's storage stack
body: Comparing stacks is hopeless unless you draw them the same way, so use six layers, bottom to top. The **DFS layer** turns thousands of disks and flash drives into one pool. The blob or object layer holds large immutable data like photos and videos. Databases hold small structured records with keys and indexes. Caches sit in front of databases to absorb reads. The lake or warehouse holds analytics data, usually columnar files. Archival keeps cold data for years at the lowest cost per byte.
takeaway: Draw every stack on the same six layers, or you compare labels, not systems.
deeper:
**What sorts data into layers:** Size, shape and temperature. A photo is big and never changes, so it goes to blob storage. A profile row is small, keyed and updated, so it lives in a database. A year of logs is scanned in bulk, so it lands in columnar lake files.

**Layers stack on each other:** At Google, Spanner stores its data in files on Colossus and BigQuery reads columnar files from Colossus. At Meta, the blob store and the data warehouse are both tenants of Tectonic. The bottom layer is often the floor under several others.

**Blanks are information:** When a company has published nothing for a layer, the comparison says so. Apple's cache and lake layers are marked not published. That is an honest blank, not an empty layer.

**Use it on your own system:** Map every datastore you run to one of the six layers. Two systems doing the same job, or a layer nobody owns, will jump out.

quiz.q: Your team stores user avatars as blobs inside a MySQL table next to profile rows. Which two layers are you mixing, and what is the usual split?
quiz.a: The blob layer and the database layer. Large immutable avatars belong in an object store; the database keeps small structured rows, such as a pointer to each object.

mcq.q: Which layer usually holds analytics data as columnar files?
options: Lake / warehouse
Archival
Blob / object
Cache
mcq.why: The lake or warehouse layer holds analytics data, usually as columnar files. Archival holds cold data kept cheaply for years.

section: How to read the stack diagrams
hook: Google, Meta and AWS each run dozens of storage systems. Underneath, most of them share just one thing.
title: One shared foundation, many specialised systems on top
body: Big companies run many databases, caches and blob stores. You would expect many separate storage pools too. Instead, most giants build a small number of **shared foundations** and put specialised systems on top. Google has Colossus, Meta has Tectonic, Azure has its stream layer, and S3 has its storage nodes. The split has a logic: the foundation is where scale and cost live, and the specialised systems are where product needs live.
takeaway: Share the bytes. Specialise the interfaces.
deeper:
**Why share the bottom:** Disks, flash, erasure coding and repair are expensive to get right and get cheaper with scale. One pool can pack IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry tenants onto the same disks, so less hardware sits idle.

**Why specialise the top:** A social graph, a photo store and a SQL ledger need different APIs, indexes and consistency. Forcing them into one database would hurt every product. So Google runs Bigtable, Spanner, Firestore and Memorystore, all over one DFS.

**The name for it:** Standardize at the bottom, polyglot at the top. Google did it with Colossus, and Meta made the same move with Tectonic ten years later.

**The catch:** A shared foundation concentrates risk. In general, a bug or bad rollout there can reach every system above it, so the foundation deserves the most careful change process. AWS, for example, checks ShardStore with formal methods.

quiz.q: Three teams each run their own HDFS cluster on identical disks. One is out of space; another is out of IOPS. What does the foundation pattern suggest?
quiz.a: Consolidate onto one shared storage pool. Pooling lets the capacity-hungry and IOPS-hungry workloads use each other's idle resource, while each team keeps its own system on top.

mcq.q: In the giants' stacks, where do scale and cost mostly live?
options: In the shared storage foundation
In the specialised databases on top
In the caching layer
In the archival tier
mcq.why: The foundation turns thousands of disks into one pool, so scale and cost live there. Specialised systems on top serve product needs.

hook: Spanner, Bigtable, BigQuery and Cloud Storage look like four products. Where do their bytes actually live?
title: At Google, almost every layer sits on Colossus
body: Google runs many storage products, yet one cluster file system holds nearly all their bytes. **Colossus**, the successor to GFS since about 2010, is the foundation. Bigtable, a wide-column store from 2006, stores its data on it. Spanner, Google's global SQL database from 2012, keeps its data in files on Colossus. BigQuery reads columnar Capacitor files from it, and Google Cloud Storage runs on it. Even Colossus's own metadata lives in Bigtable.
takeaway: Google standardizes the bottom and goes polyglot at the top.
deeper:
**The stack, bottom up:**
1. Disks and flash in D file servers.
2. Colossus, the cluster file system.
3. Bigtable, Spanner, Cloud Storage and internal blob stores.
4. F1, the Ads SQL system, on Spanner.

Around them sit in-process and memory caches in front of Bigtable and Spanner, Dremel/BigQuery for analytics, and colder media plus an Archive storage class for cold data.

**The recursion:** Colossus stores its metadata in Bigtable, and Bigtable stores its data on a smaller Colossus. The loop ends at a small, simple base.

**Why it pays:** One storage foundation per cluster serves nearly every workload, so durability and efficiency work happens once instead of once per product.

**The build extreme:** Google is the purest build company. Almost every layer, from the file system to the query engine, is in-house.

quiz.q: A Spanner database and a BigQuery table at Google both need cheaper, more durable storage. Which single system's improvements help both, and why?
quiz.a: Colossus. Spanner stores its data in files on Colossus and BigQuery reads its columnar files from Colossus, so both inherit whatever the foundation improves.

mcq.q: Where does Colossus keep its own file system metadata?
options: In Bigtable
In a single master's RAM
In Spanner
In local files on each D server
mcq.why: Colossus moved metadata into Bigtable, served by scalable Curators, so metadata scales far past GFS's single master.

hook: Google's first file system held all its metadata in one machine's RAM. Where did its successor put it?
title: GFS kept metadata in RAM. Colossus put it in Bigtable.
body: GFS (SOSP 2003) was the first cluster file system: one master, 64 MB chunks, three replicas. The single master held all metadata in memory, which capped how far a cluster could grow. Bigtable (OSDI 2006), a sorted, sparse, wide-column map, was built on top of GFS. **Colossus**, in use from about 2010 and described publicly in 2021, turned the relationship around: it stores its own metadata in Bigtable, served by scalable **Curators**.
takeaway: When one master runs out of RAM, shard the metadata into a database.
deeper:
**The lineage:**
1. GFS, 2003: one master, all metadata in RAM.
2. Bigtable, 2006: a wide-column store built on GFS.
3. Colossus, about 2010: metadata in Bigtable, Curators in front.

**The payoff:** Google said in 2021 that Colossus clusters scale to exabytes and tens of thousands of machines, with metadata scaling over 100× beyond the largest GFS clusters.

**The recursion:** Bigtable later ran on Colossus too, so the database holding Colossus's metadata stores its own data on a smaller Colossus. The loop ends at a small, simple base.

**The migration lever:** Colossus kept a client library API, so applications moved by changing libraries, not by rewriting. Google has not published a detailed migration story, but that design choice shows how a move of this size was possible.

quiz.q: Your file system's single metadata server is at 90% of its RAM, and bigger machines are running out. What did Google do in the same spot?
quiz.a: It stopped scaling one master up. Colossus moved metadata into Bigtable, a sharded store Google already ran, with scalable Curators in front, so metadata grows with shards.

mcq.q: What limit of GFS did Colossus fix by moving metadata into Bigtable?
options: One master held all metadata in RAM
Chunks were too small at 64 MB
Each chunk kept only one replica
Clients had no library API to call
mcq.why: GFS's single master kept all metadata in memory. Colossus sharded metadata into Bigtable, so it scales horizontally.

hook: Google's ads business outgrew a MySQL setup split into shards by hand. What did Google build to get out?
title: F1 on Spanner let Google Ads leave hand-sharded MySQL
body: Manually sharded MySQL works until you need to reshard. Then every split is a risky hand operation, and Google's Ads business hit exactly that wall. Google's scalable SQL came in steps. **Megastore** (CIDR 2011) added entity groups with Paxos across data centers, on Bigtable. **Spanner** (OSDI 2012) made SQL globally distributed, with external consistency from TrueTime. **F1** (VLDB 2013) was distributed SQL for Ads, built on Spanner, so Ads could leave its hard-to-reshard MySQL.
takeaway: If resharding is a manual project, sharding belongs inside the database.
deeper:
**The climb:**
1. Bigtable, 2006: a scalable wide-column map.
2. Megastore, 2011: Paxos-replicated entity groups on Bigtable.
3. Spanner, 2012: global SQL with external consistency.
4. F1, 2013: the Ads database on Spanner.

**Why resharding hurts:** With manual shards, the application decides which MySQL instance holds a row. Splitting a hot shard means copying data, updating routing and keeping writes correct during the move, all by hand. A database that shards itself does this as routine work.

**How it fits the stack:** Spanner stores its data in files on Colossus, so even Google's global SQL sits on the same foundation as everything else.

**Scope:** GFS to Colossus was Google's biggest migration. Spanner also replaced sharded MySQL for Ads, a database-level move on top of that foundation.

quiz.q: A team shards Postgres by customer ID in application code and dreads adding shards. What does Google's Ads history suggest, and what is the trade?
quiz.a: Move sharding into the database, as Ads did with F1 on Spanner. You trade a more complex distributed database for routine resharding instead of risky manual splits.

mcq.q: Why was F1 built?
options: So Ads could leave manually sharded MySQL
To replace Bigtable for web indexing
To serve as Colossus's metadata store
To run analytics over columnar files
mcq.why: F1 is distributed SQL on Spanner, built so the Ads business could escape a hand-sharded MySQL setup that was hard to reshard.

hook: Google Cloud Storage is a public product anyone can pay for. What runs underneath it?
title: BigQuery and Cloud Storage both sit on Colossus
body: Analytics and blob storage sound like separate worlds with separate hardware. At Google they share one floor. **Dremel** (VLDB 2010), public as BigQuery in 2011, is a columnar, tree-structured query engine over nested data, and it reads **Capacitor** columnar files from Colossus. Google Cloud Storage, the public object store launched in 2010, also runs on Colossus, Google says. In 2025 Google described Rapid Storage, a zonal bucket type built directly on Colossus's stateful protocol.
takeaway: One pool of bytes can serve SQL scans and object reads alike.
deeper:
**Why columnar:** Analytics queries touch a few columns across billions of rows. Storing each column together means a query reads only the columns it needs, and similar values compress well.

**Why a tree:** Dremel fans a query out through a tree of servers and merges partial results on the way back up, so a big scan runs in parallel across many machines.

**Nested data:** Dremel was designed for nested records, not only flat tables, so logs and similar data can be queried without flattening them first.

**One foundation, two products:** BigQuery and Cloud Storage expose very different APIs over the same file system, and Colossus's temperature tiering sits beneath both.

**The 2025 number:** Google says one Rapid Storage bucket supports 20 million requests per second with sub-millisecond latency. Object storage gets that fast by talking to Colossus's protocol directly.

quiz.q: An analyst's query reads 3 of 200 columns across a huge table. Why does Dremel's columnar layout make this cheap?
quiz.a: Each column is stored together, so the engine reads only those 3 columns instead of every full row, and similar values in a column compress well.

mcq.q: What does Google say Google Cloud Storage runs on?
options: Colossus
Bigtable
Spanner
A separate blob-only file system
mcq.why: Google says Cloud Storage runs on Colossus, the same cluster file system under Bigtable, Spanner and BigQuery.

hook: Google almost never says how many bytes it stores. So which numbers has it chosen to publish?
title: Colossus: exabyte clusters, 100× GFS's metadata
body: Google publishes few raw totals, so each number counts. In 2021 it said Colossus clusters scale to exabytes and tens of thousands of machines. The telling figure is metadata: it scales over 100× beyond the largest GFS clusters, because metadata moved into **Bigtable**. In 2025 Google added that one Rapid Storage zonal bucket, built on Colossus's stateful protocol, supports 20 million requests per second at sub-millisecond latency.

stat.label: metadata scale beyond the largest GFS clusters

takeaway: At exabyte scale, the proud number is metadata, not bytes.
deeper:
**Why metadata is the brag:** Adding disks is easy. Tracking billions of files, their chunks and their locations is hard, and it is exactly where GFS broke. A 100× jump in metadata scale is proof the redesign worked.

**Read the dates:** The Colossus figures are from 2021; the Rapid Storage figure is from 2025. Putting them next to S3's 2026 totals or Meta's 2021 Tectonic cluster mixes years.

**Read the units:** Exabytes measure capacity. Requests per second measure load. Metadata scale measures how many files and blocks the system can track. None of them converts into the others.

**The honest gap:** Google publishes few raw totals. A confident "Google stores X exabytes" needs a source before you repeat it. Ask for the unit, the year and the scope before any number goes on a slide.

quiz.q: A blog post says "Colossus is 100× bigger than GFS." What is wrong with that phrasing?
quiz.a: The published 100× is metadata scale, not bytes or machines. Google said Colossus metadata scales over 100× beyond the largest GFS clusters because it moved into Bigtable.

mcq.q: Why could Colossus metadata scale over 100× past GFS?
options: Metadata moved into sharded Bigtable
Masters were given far more RAM
Chunks grew from 64 MB to 1 GB
Clients cached all metadata locally
mcq.why: Moving metadata out of one master's RAM into Bigtable, served by Curators, let it scale horizontally.

predict.q: In 2025, how many requests per second did Google say a single Rapid Storage bucket supports?
options: 20 million
2 billion

hook: Google has Bigtable, Spanner, Firestore and Memorystore. How many distributed file systems do they share?
title: Many Google databases, one file system underneath
body: Google is the purest build company: almost every layer is in-house. Its key idea is layering on one foundation. GFS and then Colossus store the bytes. Bigtable stores Colossus's own metadata. Spanner stores its data in files on Colossus, and BigQuery reads columnar files from it. One foundation per cluster serves nearly every workload. That is **standardize at the bottom, polyglot at the top**, the same move Meta made with Tectonic ten years later.
takeaway: Run as many databases as you need, on one file system.
deeper:
**Why standardize the bottom:** Durability, repair, erasure coding and disk placement are hard problems. Solving them once in the foundation means every database above inherits the answer instead of reimplementing it.

**Why stay polyglot on top:** Bigtable, Spanner, Firestore and Memorystore serve different access patterns. Sharing one DFS does not force them to share an API or a consistency model.

**The recursion:** Bigtable holds Colossus's metadata while storing its own data on a smaller Colossus. The loop ends at a small, simple base.

**The trade-off:** As a general rule, a shared foundation concentrates risk. A bug or bad rollout in that layer reaches everything above it, so it deserves the most careful change process.

**Two roads, one design:** Google started with a shared foundation. Meta started specialised and consolidated onto Tectonic later. They ended up in the same place.

quiz.q: Your org runs Postgres, Cassandra and Elasticsearch, each on its own storage hardware. What would Google's philosophy change, and what would it keep?
quiz.a: It would put one shared storage foundation under them, so capacity and durability work is done once. It would keep the three databases, since polyglot on top is fine.

mcq.q: Which phrase best describes Google's storage philosophy?
options: Standardize the bottom, polyglot at the top
Polyglot at every layer, including the DFS
One database for every workload
Buy the foundation, build the databases
mcq.why: Many databases (Bigtable, Spanner, Firestore, Memorystore) share one DFS: a standard foundation with varied systems above it.

hook: Your file system's metadata server is maxed out. A bigger machine buys you months. What did Google do instead?
title: Put metadata in a database you already trust
body: GFS broke because one master held all metadata in RAM, and a bigger master only delays the wall. Colossus fixed it by storing metadata in **Bigtable**, a sharded system Google already operated, with Curators in front. Bigtable itself stores data on a smaller Colossus, and the recursion ends at a small, simple base. Meta did the same with Tectonic on ZippyDB. When your metadata service becomes the bottleneck, ask whether a sharded store you already run can hold it.
takeaway: The best new metadata store is a sharded database you already run.
deeper:
**Why metadata breaks first:** Data spreads across thousands of disks naturally. Metadata, the map of which file lives where, starts in one place because that makes it easy to keep consistent. That one place is the first thing to run out of memory.

**Why "already trust" matters:** A brand-new metadata system brings new bugs, new on-call and new failure modes. Reusing a sharded store with years of production hardening means you inherit its scaling, replication and tooling.

**How the recursion stays finite:**
1. Big Colossus stores user data.
2. Bigtable stores big Colossus's metadata.
3. Bigtable's own data sits on a smaller Colossus.
4. The loop ends at that small, simple base.

**Ask this:** When metadata is the bottleneck, which sharded system do we already operate that could hold it?

quiz.q: Your object store's metadata lives in one Postgres primary that is at its limit. You also run a mature sharded key-value store. What would the Colossus lesson suggest?
quiz.a: Move object metadata into the sharded key-value store you already operate, with a stateless service in front, so metadata scales with shards instead of one primary.

mcq.q: What is the common idea behind Colossus-on-Bigtable and Tectonic-on-ZippyDB?
options: Metadata moves into a horizontally sharded key-value store
Metadata is cached entirely in client memory
Each file stores its own metadata beside its data
A bigger single master handles all metadata
mcq.why: Both move file system metadata out of one master's memory into a sharded store, so metadata scales with the number of shards.

hook: On most clouds you pick a storage class for cold data. On Colossus, nobody picks. So who moves it?
title: Colossus tiers by temperature so users never have to
body: Most clouds make you choose: a hot class, a cold class, and lifecycle rules to move data between them. Choose badly and you pay too much or wait too long. Google's 2021 Colossus post describes a different split of duties. New, hot data goes to flash and is spread evenly over all disks. As it ages and cools, the file system moves it to larger, cheaper drives. This is **tiering by temperature**, done inside the file system, not by users.
takeaway: Tiering is the file system's job, not every user's homework.
deeper:
**Why temperature works:** Data tends to be read most right after it is written and less as it ages. Fresh data on flash serves the heavy early reads fast. Older data on big, cheap drives costs less per byte. The access pattern does the sorting.

**Why spread evenly:** If new writes all landed on a few drives, those drives would become hotspots while others sat idle. Spreading hot data over all disks shares the load.

**Where tiering lives:** Many systems push tiering to users: pick a class, write lifecycle rules, move data yourself. Google made it a file-system responsibility, so everything above Colossus gets it without extra work.

**The same instinct, twice:** Google also scales metadata out with Curators over Bigtable instead of making one master bigger. Both keep scaling automatic and invisible to applications.

**The contrast:** S3 Glacier is a set of storage classes the customer chooses.

quiz.q: Your team writes lifecycle rules to move each bucket from hot to cold storage, and half the buckets have no rules. How would Colossus-style tiering change this?
quiz.a: The storage system would move data by temperature itself, putting new data on flash and older data on cheaper drives, so buckets without rules still get tiered.

mcq.q: In Colossus, what decides when data moves to cheaper drives?
options: The file system, as the data ages and cools
The application, by choosing a storage class
A lifecycle rule each user writes
A manual request to the storage team
mcq.why: Google's 2021 post says Colossus puts new data on flash and moves colder data to larger, cheaper drives itself.

hook: A latency-critical database and a cheap archive share one file system. Who decides how each is protected?
title: In Colossus, each app picks its own durability recipe
body: One fixed durability policy forces every workload into the same trade-off. **Replication** gives fast reads and simple repair but costs space. **Erasure coding** saves space but makes writes and repairs costlier. Colossus avoids choosing for everyone: its client library does software RAID and erasure coding. Encoding happens on the client, so each application picks its own mix of durability and performance, and one file system serves both a latency-sensitive database and a cost-sensitive archive.
takeaway: Put the durability dial in the client, and one file system fits everyone.
deeper:
**The trade-off curve:** Several full copies mean any copy can serve a read, and repair is a simple copy. Erasure coding splits data into fragments plus parity, so overhead is far lower, but a repair must read several fragments and rebuild.

**Meta made the same choice:** Tectonic's client library also does the encoding. Blob storage writes replicated first and re-encodes to RS(10,4) once a block is sealed. The warehouse uses RS(9,6) for long-lived data and RS(3,3) for short-lived shuffle data.

**The second payoff, migration:** Because applications talk to Colossus through a client library API, the move from GFS worked by changing libraries rather than rewriting applications. Google has not published a detailed migration story, but the design shows the path.

**The catch:** Smart clients make the library critical code running inside every application. A bug there travels everywhere the library does.

quiz.q: One team needs low write latency; another stores petabytes of rarely read logs. Both are on Colossus. How can they get different protection?
quiz.a: The Colossus client library does the encoding, so the latency team can choose replication while the logs team chooses erasure coding for lower storage overhead.

mcq.q: Where does Colossus perform software RAID and erasure coding?
options: In the client library
In the Curators
Inside Bigtable
On the D file servers
mcq.why: Colossus encodes on the client side, which lets each application choose its own durability and performance mix.

hook: On Google Cloud, what do you have to switch on to get your data encrypted at rest?
title: Google Cloud encrypts all data at rest with no action
body: Encryption that customers must remember to enable will sometimes be forgotten. Google Cloud removes the choice: it says all customer data is encrypted at rest by default, with no action by the customer. Customers who want more control can add their own keys, called **CMEK** (customer-managed encryption keys). For **data residency**, Google offers region choice plus controls such as Assured Workloads, which keep data and workloads inside required boundaries.
takeaway: A security setting nobody has to remember is one nobody can forget.
deeper:
**What CMEK adds:** With CMEK, the customer controls the key, so rotating or revoking it controls access to the data even though Google runs the storage.

**How residency works:** Choosing a region pins where data is stored. Assured Workloads adds guardrails so data and workloads stay within required boundaries.

**The industry baseline:** Encryption at rest is now a default at all three big clouds. Since January 2023, S3 encrypts all new objects by default with S3-managed keys, with KMS keys as an option. Azure Storage encrypts all data with 256-bit AES, cannot turn it off, and accepts customer keys.

**What it does not change:** Encryption at rest protects disks and media. The provider's servers can still use keys to decrypt and process the data. End-to-end encryption, like Messenger's default or Apple's Advanced Data Protection, is what takes that ability away.

quiz.q: A regulator asks whether your Google Cloud data is encrypted at rest and who controls the key. How does your answer change with CMEK?
quiz.a: It is encrypted at rest by default either way. With CMEK you also control the key, so you can rotate or revoke it and cut off access.

mcq.q: What does CMEK add on Google Cloud?
options: Customer control over the encryption keys
Encryption at rest, which is otherwise off
End-to-end encryption Google cannot read
Automatic data residency inside the EU
mcq.why: Data is already encrypted at rest by default; CMEK lets customers supply and control their own keys.

hook: Amazon is a store and a cloud at once. How does the store side shape the cloud side's storage?
title: Amazon uses storage and sells it, to itself too
body: Amazon is two things at once: a retailer that uses storage and a cloud that sells it. The retail side famously wrote the **Dynamo** paper. The cloud side runs S3, EBS, DynamoDB, Aurora and many more. Because AWS sells storage, it must build it. Because retail is expected to use what AWS sells, the retailer doubles as an in-house customer of AWS's own services. The stack runs from AWS-designed servers and Nitro cards up to S3 Glacier archival classes.
takeaway: When you sell the product, your own business is a built-in stress test.
deeper:
**The stack, bottom up:**
1. AWS-designed servers, Nitro cards, HDD and SSD fleets.
2. S3 storage nodes running ShardStore; EBS block volumes.
3. S3 objects; DynamoDB and Aurora databases.
4. ElastiCache and MemoryDB caches.
5. A lake of S3 plus Athena, EMR, Redshift and S3 Tables; Glacier classes for archive.

**The foundation:** AWS's foundation is ShardStore storage nodes plus EBS. The bottom layer, where cost and scale live, is fully under AWS's control, as Colossus is under Google's.

**Why it matters:** Storage is literally AWS's product, the first reason any company builds storage. Retail then puts real load on it: during Amazon's Prime Day 2024, DynamoDB peaked at 146 million requests per second.

quiz.q: Why does it matter to AWS customers that Amazon retail is expected to run on AWS's own databases?
quiz.a: Retail puts real load on the same services customers buy. During Prime Day 2024, DynamoDB peaked at 146 million requests per second.

mcq.q: Which part of Amazon wrote the 2007 Dynamo paper?
options: The retail side
The AWS cloud side
The devices team
An outside university lab
mcq.why: The retail side wrote Dynamo for its shopping cart. The cloud side runs S3, EBS, DynamoDB, Aurora and more.

hook: DynamoDB is named after a famous 2007 paper. Reason about it from that paper and you'll get it wrong. Why?
title: Dynamo (2007) and DynamoDB (2012) are different designs
body: The names invite a mistake. **Dynamo**, from a 2007 SOSP paper, was Amazon's internal leaderless key-value store for the shopping cart, built on consistent hashing, sloppy quorums and vector clocks. **DynamoDB**, launched in 2012, is AWS's managed key-value and document database. Despite the shared name, it is not the same design as the 2007 paper. Its own 2022 paper names a different main goal: predictable performance over peak performance.
takeaway: Same name, different machine. Read the paper for the system you run.
deeper:
**What Dynamo did:** Any replica could accept writes. Conflicting versions were tracked with vector clocks, and sloppy quorums let writes go through even when some preferred nodes were unreachable. The goal was a shopping cart that always takes writes. LinkedIn's early Voldemort was a Dynamo-style store.

**What DynamoDB optimizes:** Its USENIX ATC 2022 paper says most design choices, such as admission control, partition splitting and global admission control, serve predictable performance.

**Its scale:** On Prime Day 2024, DynamoDB served tens of trillions of calls with a peak of 146 million requests per second.

**The practical trap:** Reason about DynamoDB from the 2007 paper and you may design around mechanisms the managed service was never described as using. Read the 2022 paper and the service docs instead.

quiz.q: An engineer designs conflict resolution around vector clocks because "DynamoDB is Dynamo." What is the flaw?
quiz.a: DynamoDB is not the same design as the 2007 Dynamo paper. Vector clocks and sloppy quorums describe Amazon's internal cart store, not the managed service built later.

mcq.q: Which pairing is correct?
options: Dynamo: internal cart store, 2007. DynamoDB: managed service, 2012.
Dynamo: managed service, 2012. DynamoDB: internal cart store, 2007.
Dynamo and DynamoDB: one design, renamed in 2012.
Dynamo: an AWS cache. DynamoDB: an AWS object store.
mcq.why: Dynamo was Amazon's 2007 internal leaderless store for the cart; DynamoDB is a separate managed database launched in 2012.

hook: S3, EBS, Glacier, Express One Zone. Four ways AWS stores bytes. What job does each one do?
title: Four AWS byte stores, from hot single-zone to archive
body: No single store is best at latency, cost and durability at once, so AWS sells several. **S3** (2006) is the object store, with strong read-after-write consistency since December 2020. **EBS** (2008) gives EC2 machines network block volumes. Glacier (2012) was archival storage and is now a set of S3 storage classes. **S3 Express One Zone** (2023) is a single-zone, low-latency S3 class for hot data. Together they span block, general object, hot and cold.
takeaway: Every storage class is one point on the cost, latency and redundancy curve.
deeper:
**What each trades:**
1. EBS: disks over the network, which databases and file systems on EC2 need.
2. S3: the general object store behind lakes, backups and application data.
3. Glacier classes: slower retrieval for the lowest cost per byte.
4. Express One Zone: data kept in one zone for lower latency, with less geographic redundancy.

**Who picks the tier:** With Glacier living inside S3 as storage classes, customers stay in one service and move data between classes. But the customer chooses the class. Google's Colossus, by contrast, tiers by temperature automatically inside the file system.

**The scale behind it:** The S3 page in 2026 shows more than 700 trillion objects and more than 200 million requests per second on average. For Prime Day 2024, Amazon provisioned 264 PB of EBS.

quiz.q: A team wants the lowest-latency S3 access for hot data and can live with single-zone storage. Which class fits, and what do they give up?
quiz.a: S3 Express One Zone. It keeps data in one zone for low latency, so they give up the multi-zone redundancy of standard S3 classes.

mcq.q: How does archival tiering on AWS differ from Google's Colossus?
options: AWS customers pick Glacier classes; Colossus tiers automatically
AWS tiers automatically; Colossus users pick classes
Both require every user to write lifecycle rules
Neither one offers any cold storage tier
mcq.why: Glacier is now a set of S3 storage classes the customer picks, while Colossus moves data by temperature inside the file system.

hook: Databases usually write full data pages. Aurora never sends them across the network. What does it send?
title: Aurora ships only the log. Storage rebuilds the pages.
body: Replicating a relational database normally means shipping data pages, logs and more across the network, again and again. Aurora (2014, paper 2017) asks which one thing fully describes a change: the **redo log record**. So only redo records cross the network, to a storage layer that keeps six replicas. Storage applies the log and builds the data pages itself. Compute and storage split apart, and far less data crosses the wire.
takeaway: Ship the log. Derive everything else.
deeper:
**Why the log is enough:** A redo record is a small description of a change. Every data page can be rebuilt by applying those records in order, so sending pages as well is redundant traffic.

**What six replicas buy:** Durability and availability even when replicas fail. Because storage is a shared service rather than a disk attached to one server, compute nodes can be replaced or added without copying the whole database.

**A parallel design:** Microsoft's Socrates, behind Azure SQL Hyperscale (SIGMOD 2019), splits SQL Server into compute, a log service and page servers over Azure Storage. Both show that separating compute from storage lets each scale on its own.

**The scale:** On Prime Day 2024, Aurora ran 6,311 instances that processed 376 billion transactions.

quiz.q: Aurora keeps six storage replicas yet cuts network traffic compared with a classic replicated database. How can both be true?
quiz.a: Only small redo log records cross the network. Storage rebuilds data pages from the log, so the bulky page writes of a traditional database never travel.

mcq.q: What does Aurora send from the database engine to its storage layer?
options: Only redo log records
Full data pages and logs
Complete table snapshots
Query results for caching
mcq.why: "The log is the database": only redo records cross the network, and the 6-way replicated storage layer builds pages from them.

hook: One subtle bug in S3's storage node code could corrupt exabytes. How does AWS change that code safely?
title: S3's storage node code is checked against a toy model
body: At exabyte scale, one corner-case bug in storage node software can damage enormous amounts of data, and ordinary unit tests miss rare crash paths. **ShardStore**, described at SOSP 2021, is the Rust key-value storage node inside S3. AWS validated it with **lightweight formal methods**: property-based testing and model checking against a simple reference model. ShardStore then replaced the earlier storage node software behind the same S3 API, so customers saw no change.
takeaway: Test the complex system against a simple one that is obviously right.
deeper:
**What a reference model is:** A deliberately simple implementation of the expected behaviour, such as a plain in-memory map. Too slow for production, but easy to believe.

**How the checking works:**
1. Generate huge numbers of random operation sequences.
2. Run each one against ShardStore and the reference model.
3. Flag any difference in results.
4. Use model checking to explore interleavings and failures systematically.

**Why lightweight:** Full formal verification of a production storage engine is extremely expensive. Checking against a model gives much of the confidence at a fraction of the cost, and it can run continuously as engineers change code.

**The payoff:** This is how AWS changes low-level storage code safely at exabyte scale. The ShardStore swap happened behind an unchanged API, the same pattern as S3's move to strong consistency.

quiz.q: Your team rewrites a storage engine and wants confidence beyond unit tests, without a full formal proof. What would ShardStore's approach look like?
quiz.a: Write a simple reference model, such as an in-memory map. Run huge numbers of random operation sequences against both, check results match, and model-check failure cases.

mcq.q: What did AWS check ShardStore against?
options: A simple reference model of expected behaviour
The previous storage node's production logs
A full mathematical proof of the Rust code
Customer bug reports filed against S3
mcq.why: Property-based testing and model checking compared ShardStore with a simple reference model: lightweight formal methods.

hook: S3 serves 200 million requests a second, and every customer is spiky. Why don't its disks melt?
title: S3: 700 trillion objects and hundreds of exabytes
body: As shown on the AWS S3 page in 2026, S3 holds more than 700 trillion objects and "hundreds of exabytes", and serves more than 200 million requests per second on average. Any one customer is spiky. But S3 spreads objects over very many disks, so each disk carries a thin slice of many customers, and at this scale the **aggregate load** smooths out.
takeaway: Pool enough spiky workloads and the total turns smooth.
deeper:
**Average, not peak:** The 200 million figure is an average. Even a small share of hot objects or noisy customers could overwhelm individual disks if their data sat together.

**Heat management:** AWS has described in re:Invent talks how objects are spread over very many disks so no single disk sees too much traffic. Independent spikes from many customers average out. Scale becomes a tool, not only a problem.

**Compare carefully:** S3's figures are fleet-wide, from 2026. Meta's 1,590 PB is one Tectonic cluster's capacity in 2021. Google's 20 million requests per second is one Rapid Storage bucket in 2025. Different scopes, units and years.

**Why AWS obsesses over safety:** At this size, spreading load, isolating failures in cells and validating node software with formal methods stop being nice-to-haves.

quiz.q: One S3 customer suddenly sends ten times its normal traffic. Why don't the disks holding its data overload?
quiz.a: S3 spreads each customer's objects over very many disks, so the burst is split thinly and averages out against many other customers' independent traffic.

mcq.q: Which S3 figure from the 2026 product page is an average, not a peak?
options: 200 million+ requests per second
700 trillion+ objects stored
Hundreds of exabytes stored
146 million requests per second
mcq.why: S3's page gives more than 200 million requests per second on average. 146 million per second is DynamoDB's Prime Day 2024 peak.

predict.q: Roughly how many objects did the S3 product page report in 2026?
options: More than 700 trillion
About 7 trillion
About 70 billion

hook: Prime Day 2024: one AWS service peaked at 146 million requests a second. Another beat it by over 100×. Which?
title: Prime Day 2024: DynamoDB at 146M/s, a cache at 1T/min
body: AWS published what Prime Day 2024, an Amazon retail sales event, demanded from its own services. DynamoDB served tens of trillions of calls, peaking at 146 million requests per second. ElastiCache served over a quadrillion requests in a day, peaking above 1 trillion requests per minute. Amazon provisioned 264 PB of **EBS** and performed 5.6 trillion EBS I/Os. Aurora ran 6,311 instances that processed 376 billion transactions. Watch the **units**: one peak is per second, the other per minute.
takeaway: Convert the units before comparing, or the biggest number lies.
deeper:
**Do the conversion:** 1 trillion requests per minute divided by 60 is over 16 billion per second. DynamoDB's 146 million is already per second. Once the units match, ElastiCache's peak is over 100× larger.

**Don't invent a relationship:** These are separate services with separate workloads. The post does not say ElastiCache sat in front of DynamoDB, so the gap proves nothing about cache hit rates.

**What each number shows:**
1. EBS: 264 PB provisioned, so plenty of work still runs on block storage.
2. Aurora: 6,311 instances, so relational databases carry real load too.
3. DynamoDB: tens of trillions of calls in one event.

**Eat your own cooking:** Prime Day is a retail event running on AWS's public services, so it stress-tests the same databases, caches and volumes customers buy.

quiz.q: A slide says DynamoDB peaked at 146 million and ElastiCache at 1 trillion, so the cache handled about 7,000× more. What is wrong?
quiz.a: Units. ElastiCache's peak is per minute, DynamoDB's per second. Converted, ElastiCache peaked above 16 billion per second, roughly 110× DynamoDB, not 7,000×.

mcq.q: About what was ElastiCache's Prime Day 2024 peak in requests per second?
options: Over 16 billion
About 1 trillion
About 146 million
About 16 million
mcq.why: Above 1 trillion requests per minute, divided by 60 seconds, is over 16 billion requests per second.

predict.q: On Prime Day 2024, which AWS service had the highest peak request rate?
options: ElastiCache
DynamoDB
Aurora

hook: Amazon's retailer ran on thousands of databases bought from an outside vendor. What did it take to leave them?
title: Amazon retail moved 75 PB off 7,500 Oracle databases
body: Amazon's own retailer ran on about 7,500 Oracle databases, a bought product at the heart of the business. In 2019 the consumer business finished moving 75 PB to AWS services such as DynamoDB, Aurora and Redshift. It used **AWS Database Migration Service** for the data. The hard part was the model: many schemas were rewritten to fit **key-value** designs, not just copied.
takeaway: Moving data is the tool's job. Remodelling it is yours.
deeper:
**Why schemas changed:** Oracle is relational. DynamoDB is a key-value and document store. Moving between them means joins and ad hoc queries give way to access patterns designed around keys, so many schemas were rewritten rather than copied.

**Many destinations:** DynamoDB, Aurora and Redshift were among the targets. The exit did not swap one database for one database, which fits AWS's polyglot, right-tool-for-the-job stance.

**Why it is the proof:** AWS builds what it sells, and Amazon retail is expected to use it. A retailer moving 75 PB off a bought database onto its own cloud's databases is the strongest form of eating your own cooking.

**The credibility angle:** A cloud that asks customers to trust its databases makes a stronger case when its own retail business runs on them.

quiz.q: A team plans to move an Oracle schema to DynamoDB with a data migration tool and no redesign. What did Amazon's own exit suggest they are missing?
quiz.a: Data modelling. Amazon used Database Migration Service to move the data but rewrote many schemas to fit key-value access patterns, because relational joins don't map directly.

mcq.q: Besides AWS Database Migration Service, what did Amazon's Oracle exit require?
options: Rewriting many schemas for key-value models
Keeping Oracle as the permanent source of truth
Moving all 75 PB into one Aurora cluster
Buying a second commercial database license
mcq.why: The tool moved the data, but many schemas were rewritten to fit key-value models on services like DynamoDB.

hook: AWS sells key-value, relational, document, graph, time-series and ledger databases. Who pays for the choice?
title: AWS is polyglot on purpose, and customers must choose well
body: Google hides many databases behind one foundation. AWS puts the menu up front. It sells many **purpose-built databases**: key-value, relational, document, graph, time series and ledger. The official line is "use the right tool for the job", and each service fits its access pattern well. The trade-off is that customers must pick well, and a wrong pick is their cost. Underneath, AWS builds everything it sells, and Amazon retail is expected to use it: **eat your own cooking**.
takeaway: A menu of perfect tools is only as good as the person ordering.
deeper:
**The strength:** Fit. A graph workload on a graph database, a ledger on a ledger database, key-value on DynamoDB, relational on Aurora. Each can be tuned for one access pattern instead of compromising for all.

**The weakness:** Decision burden and sprawl. A team can pick the wrong database, and an organisation can end up running a dozen databases with a dozen operational playbooks.

**When polyglot is fine:** When a handful of teams use storage, polyglot by team works. When hundreds do, a shared foundation plus an abstraction layer beats one-off choices, which is how Meta, Google and Netflix operate.

**The proof of cooking:** In 2019 Amazon retail moved off about 7,500 Oracle databases onto AWS's own DynamoDB, Aurora and Redshift. The seller became the customer.

**Ask this:** Who in your organisation owns the choice of database, and who pays when it is wrong?

quiz.q: Your company has 300 teams on AWS, each picking its own database service. What trade-off appears, and what do Meta, Google and Netflix do instead?
quiz.a: Sprawl: hundreds of separate choices and playbooks, and every migration touches every team. At that scale a shared foundation plus an abstraction layer beats one-off picks.

mcq.q: What is AWS's official line on its many database services?
options: Use the right tool for the job
One database should serve every workload
Customers should build their own engines
Pick the cheapest database available
mcq.why: AWS is polyglot on purpose, selling purpose-built databases, with the trade-off that customers must choose well.

hook: DynamoDB's designers picked one goal over raw speed and let it drive almost every design choice. Which goal?
title: DynamoDB chose predictable performance over peak speed
body: A multi-tenant database that is usually fast but sometimes stalls forces every customer to add retries, timeouts and spare capacity. The DynamoDB paper (USENIX ATC 2022) says the team chose **predictable performance** over peak performance as its main goal. Most design choices serve it: **admission control**, partition splitting and global admission control. The lesson for anyone designing a shared storage service: choose one primary goal like this and write it down.
takeaway: Write down one primary goal. It settles a thousand design arguments.
deeper:
**How each mechanism serves it:**
1. Admission control limits how much work a partition accepts, so one tenant cannot overload shared resources.
2. Partition splitting divides hot or growing partitions so load spreads.
3. Global admission control coordinates limits across the fleet rather than per node.

**Why predictability wins for shared services:** Customers plan around your worst case, not your best. Consistent latency lets them size their own systems honestly.

**Why write it down:** Shared storage faces endless trade-offs: latency or throughput, cost or durability, features or simplicity. Without a written primary goal, each decision gets argued from scratch and the system drifts. With one, most debates reduce to a single question: does this make performance more predictable?

**The scale it reached:** DynamoDB peaked at 146 million requests per second on Prime Day 2024.

quiz.q: A teammate proposes a change that doubles peak throughput for a DynamoDB-style service but adds occasional multi-second stalls. How would DynamoDB's written goal decide it?
quiz.a: Reject or redesign it. The primary goal is predictable performance over peak, so extra peak speed that brings unpredictable stalls works against the goal.

mcq.q: According to its 2022 paper, what was DynamoDB's main design goal?
options: Predictable performance over peak performance
Peak throughput for the largest tenants
The lowest cost per stored byte
Full SQL compatibility with joins
mcq.why: The team chose predictable over peak performance; admission control, partition splitting and global admission control serve that goal.

hook: A bad deploy hits AWS. Why does it take down some customers and not all of them?
title: AWS splits services into cells so failures stay small
body: Any shared service will eventually meet a bad deploy, a software bug or a hardware fault. The question is how many customers feel it. AWS splits services into **cells**, independent slices of infrastructure, so one failure hits a slice of customers, not all. Inside S3, **heat management** tackles the other risk, hotspots: objects are spread over very many disks so no single disk sees too much traffic. Cells contain failures; wide spreading contains load.
takeaway: Decide how much may fail together before it fails together.
deeper:
**Cells limit blast radius:** If a fault hits one cell, only that cell's customers are affected. In general, changes can also roll out cell by cell, so a bad change is caught while it touches a slice, not the fleet.

**Heat management smooths load:** Any single customer's traffic is bursty: a viral file, a batch job. If that data sat on a few disks, they would overload while others idled. Spread over very many disks, each disk carries a small share of many customers, and the spikes average out. AWS has described this in re:Invent talks.

**Two questions, two answers:** Cells answer "how much can fail together?" Heat management answers "how much can one customer load one disk?"

**A relative:** Azure's storage stamps apply a similar idea to storage: fixed-size units that cap how much fails together, grown by adding more of them.

quiz.q: Your multi-tenant service runs as one big cluster, and last month one bad config took down every customer. Which AWS idea addresses this, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: Cells: split the service into independent slices so a failure hits one slice. The cost is more units to operate and some capacity stranded inside each cell.

mcq.q: What does S3's heat management spread across very many disks?
options: Objects, so no single disk gets too much traffic
Customers, each on its own dedicated disk
Metadata only, leaving the data in place
Backups, copied to separate Regions
mcq.why: Objects are spread widely so each disk carries a small share of many customers' traffic, and the spikes average out.

hook: In December 2020, every S3 application got a stronger guarantee overnight. What did customers have to change?
title: S3 went strongly consistent with no API or price change
body: Before December 2020, an app that wrote an S3 object and read it right back could see stale results, so many teams built workarounds. Then S3 moved to **strong read-after-write consistency** without any API change and without any price change. Every existing application got the stronger guarantee on the same day, with no client migration. It is the model for **upgrading the contract in place**: improve what lies beneath while customers keep exactly the same interface.
takeaway: The cheapest migration for users is the one they never notice.
deeper:
**The workarounds that died:** Retries, extra metadata stores and deliberate delays existed to cope with stale reads. After the change, a read after a successful write returns the new data, so that code became unnecessary.

**Why in place beats a new API:** The alternative, a new API or storage class with stronger guarantees, would make every customer change code and move data. At S3's scale that could take years, and many would never finish. Upgrading the existing contract reached everyone at once.

**Where the difficulty went:** Entirely to the provider. Strengthening guarantees under a huge live system, without raising prices, is hard engineering.

**A sibling move:** ShardStore also replaced S3's earlier storage node software behind the same API. Owning the internals, including node software checked with formal methods, gives AWS room for changes like these.

quiz.q: You run an internal blob service with eventual consistency, and 40 teams have built retry hacks around it. How would S3's 2020 approach have you strengthen it?
quiz.a: Make reads strongly consistent behind the existing API and pricing. Every team benefits at once with no migration, and their workarounds become unnecessary rather than required.

mcq.q: What did S3 customers have to change to get strong consistency in 2020?
options: Nothing: no API or price change
Switch to a new strongly consistent API
Move their data to a new storage class
Pay a higher price per request
mcq.why: S3 upgraded the contract in place: same API, same price, a stronger guarantee for every existing application on the same day.

hook: Two AWS migrations needed zero customer work. A third needed many schema rewrites. What made the difference?
title: Change the internals, keep the interface
body: Not all migrations cost the same, and the interface decides who pays. S3's move to strong consistency in 2020 changed nothing customers saw: same API, same price. **ShardStore** replaced S3's storage node software, again behind the same API. Both were invisible. Amazon retail's 2019 exit from Oracle was the opposite: the interface itself changed, so teams used AWS Database Migration Service and rewrote many schemas to fit key-value models. When the **interface** holds still, only the provider works.
takeaway: Keep the interface still and only the provider has to move.
deeper:
**Below a stable API:** In the S3 cases, the contract customers depended on stayed the same or got strictly better. That is the cheapest migration for users and the hardest for the provider.

**Changing the interface:** The Oracle exit moved from a relational database to purpose-built services like DynamoDB, Aurora and Redshift, across about 7,500 databases and 75 PB. The migration service moved data; the modelling work could not be automated away.

**The same instinct elsewhere:**
1. Google moved GFS to Colossus by keeping a client library API.
2. Uber moved bytes to Google Cloud behind an HDFS-compatible connector.
3. Netflix built a KV abstraction layer so backend moves become platform tasks.

**Ask this:** Before a migration, where is the interface, and which side of it does the change fall on?

quiz.q: You must replace your storage engine and also want to change how clients query data. Following AWS's pattern, how would you sequence it?
quiz.a: Swap the engine behind the existing interface first, so clients notice nothing. Change the query interface later as a separate, visible migration with its own rewrites.

mcq.q: Why did the Oracle exit need schema rewrites while S3's consistency upgrade needed none?
options: The Oracle exit changed the interface itself
The Oracle exit moved far more data than S3
S3 waited until every customer agreed
S3 customers rewrote their code in advance
mcq.why: S3 changed internals behind a stable API; leaving Oracle for key-value services changed the data model teams programmed against.

hook: An auditor asks if your oldest S3 buckets are encrypted by default. Why is "yes" not safe to assume?
title: S3 encrypts new objects by default, since January 2023
body: A forgotten setting is a common source of unencrypted data. Since January 2023, S3 encrypts all **new objects** by default with S3-managed keys, called **SSE-S3**. Customers can choose KMS keys instead for more control. The word "new" matters: the default says nothing about objects written before it. On residency, data stays in the Region the customer picks. S3 does not move it to other Regions unless the customer sets up replication.
takeaway: Read the date on every default. Old data predates new promises.
deeper:
**What SSE-S3 fixes:** Every new object is encrypted at rest without customer action, which removes the forgotten-setting failure.

**Why choose KMS keys:** Customer-chosen keys give control over key policies, rotation and revocation, which many compliance regimes prefer.

**The residency promise:** Data does not leave the chosen Region unless the customer configures replication. So the reasoning is simple: pick a Region inside the required jurisdiction and do not replicate outside it. This is the base of most AWS data residency stories.

**Peers:** Google Cloud encrypts all customer data at rest by default and offers CMEK. Azure Storage encrypts all data with 256-bit AES by default, cannot turn it off, and accepts customer keys.

**The limit:** At-rest encryption protects media, not access. The provider's servers can still use keys to decrypt and serve data.

quiz.q: A company must keep EU customer data inside the EU on S3. What is the simplest setup, and what would break it?
quiz.a: Store the data in an EU Region. S3 keeps data in the chosen Region, so the main risk is setting up replication to a Region outside the EU.

mcq.q: Since January 2023, what does S3 do with new objects by default?
options: Encrypts them with S3-managed keys (SSE-S3)
Encrypts them with customer KMS keys
Replicates them to a second Region
Leaves them unencrypted until configured
mcq.why: S3 applies SSE-S3 to all new objects by default; customers may choose KMS keys instead.

hook: Meta stores photos, a data warehouse and AI checkpoints. How many distributed file systems hold them all?
title: Meta's stack: one file system under photos and warehouse
body: Meta once ran a separate storage system for each big workload. Today one exabyte-scale file system, **Tectonic**, sits at the bottom, used from about 2017 onward. Its blob storage tenant replaced Haystack and f4, and its data warehouse tenant replaced HDFS. Above it, MySQL with **MyRocks** holds the social graph, ZippyDB offers Paxos key-value on RocksDB, and TAO plus a Memcache fleet absorb reads. Presto, Spark and Hive run the warehouse.
takeaway: Meta ended up where Google started: one floor, many rooms.
deeper:
**The stack, bottom up:**
1. OCP servers with HDD and flash.
2. Tectonic, one DFS for many tenants.
3. Tenants: blob storage and the data warehouse.
4. MySQL/MyRocks (UDB) and ZippyDB for structured data.
5. TAO and Memcache in front, to absorb reads.

**The tenants:** Blob storage replaced Haystack (2010) and f4 (2014). The warehouse tenant replaced HDFS and runs Presto, Spark and Hive on top. Colder tiers and cold storage halls hold archival data.

**Build and share:** Meta runs its own data centers and open-sources a lot, including RocksDB, MyRocks, Presto and, originally, Cassandra.

**The payoff:** Moving the data warehouse from HDFS to Tectonic cut the number of warehouse clusters by 10×.

**The lesson:** Meta specialised first to learn each workload, then consolidated once stranded capacity became the bigger cost.

quiz.q: Meta's photos and its analytics warehouse have very different access patterns. Why can they share one file system?
quiz.a: Each Tectonic tenant chooses its own client-side encoding, and all share one pool, so IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry workloads balance each other instead of stranding resources.

mcq.q: Which systems did Tectonic replace?
options: Haystack, f4 and HDFS
TAO, Memcache and ZippyDB
MySQL, MyRocks and RocksDB
Presto, Spark and Hive
mcq.why: By 2021 Tectonic had completely replaced Haystack and f4 for blobs and HDFS for the warehouse.

hook: Meta held 260 billion photos in 2010. Why was storing each one as its own file the real bottleneck?
title: Haystack packed photos; f4 cut warm copies to 2.1×
body: A file per photo means a metadata lookup per photo, and at billions of photos that I/O dominates. **Haystack** (OSDI 2010) packed many photos into large files, holding over 260 billion images, about 20 PB, by 2010. Most photos cool fast, so **f4** (OSDI 2014) became the warm store: Reed-Solomon (10,4) plus XOR across data centers, holding over 65 PB with effective replication 2.1 instead of 3.6.
takeaway: Hot data pays for speed. Warm data should pay only for bytes.
deeper:
**Why packing works:** Opening a separate file means reading its metadata from disk before reading the photo. Packing many photos into one large file keeps the index small enough to hold in memory, so a photo read becomes close to one disk read.

**The 2010 intake:** About 1 billion new photos, roughly 60 TB, arrived every week.

**Why f4 is cheaper:** RS(10,4) stores 10 data fragments plus 4 parity fragments, and XOR across data centers protects against losing a site. That brought effective replication from 3.6 to 2.1, a large saving across 65 PB.

**The limit:** Each system fit its workload, but each wasted a different resource. Haystack ran short of IOPS while f4 had IOPS to spare, which is why both were later folded into Tectonic.

quiz.q: A warm photo tier holds 65 PB of logical data. Roughly how much raw storage does effective replication 2.1 save compared with 3.6?
quiz.a: About 97 PB. At 3.6× it needs about 234 PB raw; at 2.1× about 137 PB.

mcq.q: What was Haystack's core trick?
options: Packing many photos into large files to cut metadata I/O
Erasure-coding every photo with RS(10,4)
Caching every photo in the Memcache fleet
Storing each photo as its own small file
mcq.why: Haystack packed many photos into large files, so fetching one no longer required separate metadata reads.

hook: Meta's social graph takes about a billion reads per second. How much of that load ever reaches MySQL?
title: TAO and Memcache keep a billion reads a second off MySQL
body: A social feed reads far more than it writes, and no MySQL fleet could serve those reads directly. Meta puts two layers in front. **TAO** (USENIX ATC 2013), a graph-aware, geographically distributed cache and store over MySQL, handles about a billion reads per second and millions of writes per second. **Memcache** (NSDI 2013) scaled memcached into a regional, multi-cluster cache. Together they absorb most reads, so MySQL sees mostly writes and cache misses.
takeaway: Let the caches take the reads so the database can keep the truth.
deeper:
**Why graph-aware:** A generic cache stores opaque keys. TAO understands objects and the associations between them, like friendships and likes, so it can answer graph queries directly and keep related data together.

**Why regional and multi-cluster:** Scaling memcached from one cluster to many, across regions, raises new problems, such as keeping copies consistent when the database changes and surviving floods of misses when a cache is cold.

**What MySQL is left with:** Mostly writes and the reads that miss the caches. That changes how you size it: write throughput and storage efficiency matter more than read capacity.

**Next door:** UDB, the MySQL social graph database under TAO, later became bound by space on flash while CPU and I/O sat idle. That is why Meta moved it to MyRocks, which compresses much better.

quiz.q: Your MySQL fleet sits behind caches that absorb nearly all reads. Which resources would you watch most on the database, and why?
quiz.a: Write throughput and storage space. With most reads absorbed, the database mainly handles writes and cache misses, as MySQL does behind TAO and Memcache.

mcq.q: What does MySQL mostly see at Meta, given TAO and Memcache in front?
options: Writes and cache misses
Every read and every write
Only analytics queries
Only photo blobs
mcq.why: TAO and Memcache absorb most reads, leaving MySQL mostly writes and the reads that miss the caches.

hook: Meta's social graph database and its general key-value store share one engine underneath. Which one?
title: MyRocks and ZippyDB both run on RocksDB, an LSM tree
body: Building a storage engine from scratch for each database is slow and risky, so Meta reuses one. **RocksDB**, an LSM-tree engine that Meta open-sources, sits under both. **MyRocks** is MySQL with RocksDB as its storage engine; moving UDB, the social graph database, to it in 2017 halved UDB's storage. **ZippyDB**, described in 2021, is a general-purpose, strongly consistent key-value store that puts Paxos replication on top of RocksDB.
takeaway: Reuse one great engine. Build replication and APIs around it.
deeper:
**Why an LSM tree compresses well:** An LSM tree writes data in large sorted batches and merges them in the background, so it can compress big blocks and avoid the fragmentation of update-in-place B-trees. MyRocks halved UDB's storage compared with InnoDB.

**Why UDB needed it:** UDB was space-bound on flash while CPU and I/O sat idle. Spending some CPU on compression used the idle resource to relieve the scarce one.

**ZippyDB's layering:** RocksDB stores data on one node. Paxos keeps replicas in agreement. The result is a strongly consistent key-value service without writing a new engine.

**ZippyDB's second job:** Tectonic stores its hash-partitioned metadata in ZippyDB, so this RocksDB-based store also sits under Meta's file system.

**The open-source habit:** Meta open-sources RocksDB, MyRocks and Presto.

quiz.q: Your MySQL fleet is out of flash space, yet CPU and disk I/O are mostly idle. What does Meta's UDB case suggest, and why does it fit?
quiz.a: Switch to a better-compressing engine like MyRocks. It spends idle CPU on compression to free the scarce resource, flash space; UDB's storage halved.

mcq.q: What does ZippyDB add on top of RocksDB?
options: Paxos replication for strong consistency
A SQL layer compatible with MySQL
A graph-aware read cache
Erasure coding across data centers
mcq.why: ZippyDB is a general-purpose, strongly consistent key-value store built on RocksDB with Paxos replication.

hook: By 2021, one Meta file system had replaced three others. How can one system serve such different tenants?
title: Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system, many tenants
body: Separate storage systems per workload strand resources. **Tectonic** (FAST 2021) is one exabyte-scale DFS shared by many tenants, and it replaced Haystack, f4 and HDFS. One multitenant production cluster had 1,590 PB of capacity, 1,250 PB used, 10.7 billion files, 15 billion blocks and 4,208 storage nodes. It works because metadata is disaggregated into ZippyDB and each tenant's **client library** picks its own encoding.
takeaway: One pool serves many tenants when each tenant keeps its own recipe.
deeper:
**How it serves different tenants:**
1. Metadata splits into Name, File and Block layers, each hash-partitioned and stored in ZippyDB.
2. The client library does the encoding, so blob storage and the warehouse use different recipes.
3. All tenants share the same disks, so IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry work balance out.

**The warehouse win:** Moving the data warehouse from HDFS to Tectonic cut the number of warehouse clusters by 10×.

**How long it ran:** The paper says Tectonic had run in single-tenant clusters for several years, completely replacing Haystack, f4 and HDFS by 2021.

**Fill level:** 1,250 PB used out of 1,590 PB is roughly four-fifths full, across 4,208 storage nodes. That is one cluster, in one year; it is not Meta's total storage.

quiz.q: The Tectonic cluster had 10.7 billion files and 15 billion blocks. Why does the metadata design matter more than the 1,590 PB figure?
quiz.a: Tracking billions of files and blocks is what breaks single-master file systems. Tectonic spreads that metadata across hash-partitioned layers in ZippyDB, so it scales with shards.

mcq.q: How did moving Meta's warehouse from HDFS to Tectonic change its cluster count?
options: Cut it by 10×
Doubled it
Cut it by half
Left it unchanged
mcq.why: Meta reported that moving the data warehouse from HDFS to Tectonic cut the number of warehouse clusters by 10×.

hook: Meta spent years building a custom storage system for each workload. Then it abandoned the idea. Why?
title: Meta specialized for years, then consolidated to one DFS
body: From 2010 to 2016 Meta ran a custom system per workload: **Haystack** for hot photos, f4 for warm photos, HDFS for the warehouse. From 2017 onward it moved all of them onto one DFS, Tectonic. The Tectonic paper's reason is sharp: specialised systems **strand resources**. Each fleet ran short of one resource while wasting another, and one shared pool lets their needs cancel out.
takeaway: Specialize to learn the workload. Consolidate when idle capacity costs more.
deeper:
**Why specialize first:** Early on, each workload is poorly understood. A dedicated system lets a team learn its access pattern and tune for it, which is how Haystack's packed files and f4's erasure coding came about.

**Why consolidate later:** Once the workloads are understood, the biggest cost is capacity that sits idle. Haystack had spare disk space but not enough IOPS. f4 had spare IOPS but less space. Each wasted what the other needed.

**What one pool fixes:** IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry tenants on the same disks use each other's spare resource, so fewer disks do the same work.

**The proof:** By 2021 Tectonic had completely replaced Haystack, f4 and HDFS, and moving the warehouse alone cut warehouse clusters by 10×.

**The general arc:** Specialize-then-consolidate is a common pattern, not a Meta quirk.

quiz.q: A startup builds one general storage system for every workload on day one, citing Meta's Tectonic. What does Meta's arc say they may be skipping?
quiz.a: The specialize phase. Meta learned each workload through dedicated systems first; consolidation paid off later, once stranded capacity became the biggest cost.

mcq.q: What does "stranded resources" mean in Meta's case?
options: Each fleet wasted the resource the other lacked
Disks sat unpowered in cold storage halls
Data was lost when a region went offline
Engineers were stuck maintaining old code
mcq.why: Haystack had spare capacity but lacked IOPS; f4 had spare IOPS but less space. Each wasted what the other needed.

hook: Meta's photo store was designed for 3.6 copies' worth of disk per photo. It ended up paying for 5.3. Why?
title: Haystack ran out of IOPS, so replication climbed to 5.3×
body: Haystack held hot photos, and hot data is read constantly. It became **IOPS-bound**: it had spare disk space but not enough I/O. The only fix inside Haystack was more disks for their IOPS, which left much of their capacity empty. Its **effective replication factor** climbed from an ideal 3.6× to 5.3×. Meanwhile f4 had the opposite problem: lots of spare IOPS, less space. Tectonic put both on one shared pool, so their needs balance out.
takeaway: When one fleet lacks IOPS and another lacks space, merge them.
deeper:
**What effective replication means:** Raw bytes on disk divided by logical bytes stored. A design might target 3.6×, but if you add disks you cannot fill, the real ratio rises. At 5.3×, every photo costs almost half again as much disk as planned.

**Why disks strand:** A disk comes with fixed capacity and fixed IOPS. A hot workload uses up the IOPS long before the capacity. A warm workload does the reverse.

**How Tectonic fixes it:**
1. Put hot and warm tenants on the same disks.
2. The hot tenant uses the IOPS the warm one leaves idle.
3. The warm tenant fills the space the hot one leaves empty.

**The warning sign:** One fleet bound by IOPS while another fleet with the same disks is bound by capacity. See both, and consolidation will likely pay.

quiz.q: Fleet A is 95% busy on IOPS but 40% full. Fleet B is 20% busy but 90% full. Both use the same disks. What would Tectonic do, and why?
quiz.a: Merge them onto one shared pool. A's I/O-heavy data uses B's idle IOPS, and B's bulk data fills A's empty space, so fewer disks do the same work.

mcq.q: Why did Haystack's effective replication factor rise to 5.3×?
options: Disks added for IOPS left capacity unused
It kept extra copies of every photo for safety
RS(10,4) encoding added parity overhead
Deleted photos were never reclaimed
mcq.why: Haystack was IOPS-bound. Extra disks bought I/O but their space sat unused, raising raw bytes per logical byte from 3.6× to 5.3×.

predict.q: Haystack's ideal effective replication factor was 3.6×. What did it actually climb to?

hook: Two fleets use identical disks. One is maxed out, the other half idle. Which signal says merge them?
title: One fleet IOPS-bound, another capacity-bound: consolidate
body: "Specialize, then consolidate" is a common arc, and the hard part is knowing when to switch. Specialization wins early because you learn the workload. Consolidation wins later because **stranded capacity** becomes the biggest cost. The warning sign is exactly Meta's: one fleet is bound by **IOPS** while another fleet with the same disks is bound by capacity. Each is buying hardware for the resource it lacks while paying for the one it wastes.
takeaway: Two half-used fleets are one fully used fleet waiting to happen.
deeper:
**Why the signal is so clear:** Disks come in a fixed ratio of capacity to IOPS. Workloads do not. A hot workload wants IOPS; a cold one wants space. Run them apart and each leaves the other's resource idle.

**What to measure:** For each fleet, track both IOPS utilisation and capacity utilisation. A fleet near its limit on one while low on the other is stranding hardware.

**Why not consolidate on day one:** Early on you do not yet know each workload's shape. Dedicated systems let teams learn and tune, as Haystack and f4 did.

**The counterweight:** Consolidation grows the failure domain. Azure's stamps keep units small on purpose, trading some stranded capacity for a smaller blast radius. Ask which cost dominates for you.

**Ask this:** Are any of our fleets full on one resource and idle on the other?

quiz.q: Your team wants a third dedicated cluster for a new hot workload. The existing archive cluster uses 15% of its IOPS. What would you ask first?
quiz.a: Could the hot workload share the archive cluster's disks? The archive has idle IOPS the hot workload needs, so pooling may avoid buying stranded hardware, if the larger blast radius is acceptable.

mcq.q: When does consolidation start to beat specialization, per Meta's lesson?
options: When stranded capacity becomes the biggest cost
As soon as a second workload appears
When each workload needs its own API
When teams want independent deploys
mcq.why: Specialization wins early by teaching you the workload; consolidation wins once idle, stranded resources become the dominant cost.

hook: One Tectonic cluster tracks 10.7 billion files and 15 billion blocks. Where does all that metadata live?
title: Tectonic splits metadata into three layers in ZippyDB
