body: A single metadata server cannot track billions of files and blocks. **Tectonic** splits metadata into Name, File and Block layers, each **hash-partitioned** and stored in ZippyDB, Meta's Paxos key-value store on RocksDB. Each layer scales out on its own. It is the same idea as Colossus storing its metadata in Bigtable: move metadata out of one master and into a sharded store.
takeaway: Split metadata by what it describes, then shard each part.
deeper:
**What each layer holds:** In general terms, the Name layer maps paths and directories to files, the File layer maps files to their blocks, and the Block layer maps blocks to the storage nodes holding them. A lookup walks down the layers in that order.

**Why split them:** Each layer has its own size and access pattern. Separating them lets each be partitioned and scaled independently instead of sharing one bottleneck.

**Why hash-partition:** Hashing spreads keys evenly across ZippyDB shards, so no single shard carries a hot directory alone.

**Why ZippyDB:** It is a strongly consistent key-value store Meta already runs. Reusing it follows the rule of putting metadata in a database you already trust.

**The shared lesson:** Metadata scaling drove the biggest redesigns. GFS to Colossus and HDFS to Tectonic both moved metadata into a sharded key-value store.

quiz.q: A file system's single metadata server chokes on billions of blocks. How would Tectonic's design spread the load?
quiz.a: Split metadata into Name, File and Block layers, hash-partition each, and store them in a sharded, strongly consistent key-value store like ZippyDB, so each layer scales out separately.

mcq.q: Where does Tectonic store its metadata?
options: In ZippyDB, hash-partitioned by layer
In one master's memory
In Bigtable, behind Curators
In MySQL running MyRocks
mcq.why: Tectonic's Name, File and Block layers are each hash-partitioned and stored in ZippyDB.

hook: Meta's photos and its analytics shuffle files share one file system, yet are encoded differently. Why?
title: One file system, a different durability recipe per tenant
body: Different data has different lifetimes and write patterns, so one encoding cannot fit all. In **Tectonic**, the client library does the encoding, per tenant. Blob storage writes replicated first and re-encodes to **RS(10,4)** once a block is sealed. The warehouse uses RS(9,6) for long-lived data and RS(3,3) for short-lived shuffle data. One DFS, different durability recipes, each matched to how its data is written and how long it lives.
takeaway: Share the disks, not the encoding.
deeper:
**Why replicate first for blobs:** Small appends to an erasure-coded block are awkward, because each change touches parity. Replicating while a block is still growing keeps writes simple. Once the block is sealed and stops changing, re-encoding to RS(10,4) cuts the overhead.

**Why RS(9,6) for long-lived warehouse data:** Nine data fragments plus six parity fragments is about 1.67× overhead, with room to lose six fragments. That suits data kept a long time.

**Why RS(3,3) for shuffle:** Shuffle data lives briefly. Three data plus three parity fragments keeps encoding and repair cheap, at 2× overhead, for data that will soon be deleted.

**The Google parallel:** Colossus also encodes in the client library, so each application picks its own durability and performance mix.

**The design rule:** Put the encoding choice where knowledge of the data lives, in the tenant's client.

quiz.q: Blob storage appends small writes to a block for a while, then seals it. Why replicate first and erasure-code later instead of encoding from the start?
quiz.a: Small appends to an erasure-coded block keep touching parity, which is slow and complex. Replication handles the growing block simply; after sealing, RS(10,4) cuts overhead.

mcq.q: Which encoding does Meta's warehouse use for short-lived shuffle data?
options: Triple replication
mcq.why: The warehouse uses RS(9,6) for long-lived data and RS(3,3) for short-lived shuffle; blobs re-encode to RS(10,4) once sealed.

hook: Meta swapped the storage engine under its main user database. What made the swap safe to undo at every step?
title: InnoDB to MyRocks: a migration Meta could always undo
body: In 2017 UDB, Meta's social graph database, was space-bound on flash while CPU and I/O sat idle, and MyRocks compresses much better. So Meta moved it from InnoDB to MyRocks in steps. **MyRocks** instances first joined as replicas, were validated with checksums and **shadow queries**, then were promoted to primary. InnoDB and MyRocks could replicate each other, so rollback was always possible.
takeaway: If you cannot roll back, you are not migrating. You are gambling.
deeper:
**Why replicas first:** A new engine joining as a replica takes no production writes of its own. If it misbehaves, you drop it and nothing is lost.

**Why checksums and shadow queries:** Checksums show the data matches on both engines. Shadow queries send real read traffic to the new engine and compare answers without users seeing them, catching behaviour differences that data checks miss.

**Why two-way replication matters:** Because InnoDB and MyRocks could replicate each other, an InnoDB replica stayed current even after a MyRocks primary took writes. Rolling back meant promoting it again.

**The payoff:** MyRocks halved UDB's storage, using the CPU that had been sitting idle to compress data.

**The pattern elsewhere:** Uber's GCP move and Dropbox's S3 exit also relied on dual running and gradual cutover.

quiz.q: A week after promotion, your MyRocks primary returns wrong results. With Meta's setup, what is your recovery move, and why is it available?
quiz.a: Promote an InnoDB replica back to primary. InnoDB and MyRocks replicated each other, so the InnoDB copy stayed current even after the switch.

mcq.q: Why did Meta move UDB from InnoDB to MyRocks?
options: UDB was out of flash space; MyRocks compresses better
UDB was CPU-bound; MyRocks uses less CPU
InnoDB could not replicate across regions
MyRocks added SQL features UDB lacked
mcq.why: UDB ran out of flash space while CPU and I/O sat idle, and MyRocks's better compression halved its storage.

hook: Meta's AI clusters needed storage for checkpoints and training data. Did it build a new system?
title: Meta's AI training storage is Tectonic on flash
body: New hardware tiers tempt teams to build new storage systems. Meta mostly didn't. By 2021 Tectonic had run in single-tenant clusters for several years, completely replacing Haystack, f4 and HDFS. In 2024, Meta's GenAI clusters used a **FUSE API** backed by a flash-optimised version of Tectonic for checkpoints and data loading, plus a **Hammerspace** parallel NFS for interactive work. Same foundation, new hardware tier.
takeaway: A good foundation absorbs new hardware tiers instead of being replaced.
deeper:
**Why a FUSE API:** FUSE lets a storage system appear as an ordinary mounted file system. Training code can read data and write checkpoints with normal file operations instead of a special client.

**Why flash:** Checkpointing writes large amounts of state quickly, and data loading must keep accelerators fed. Flash serves both much faster than hard drives.

**Why Hammerspace too:** Interactive work goes to a Hammerspace parallel NFS, while checkpoints and data loading go to Tectonic on flash. Each access style gets its own path.

**The arc:**
1. 2010: Haystack for hot photos.
2. 2014: f4 for warm photos.
3. 2017 onward: Tectonic for everything.
4. 2024: Tectonic on flash for AI.

**The lesson:** Consolidation pays twice: once in efficiency, and again when new workloads arrive and find a foundation ready.

quiz.q: Your company adds a GPU cluster, and a team proposes a brand-new storage system for checkpoints. What did Meta do instead, and what is the argument for it?
quiz.a: Meta extended its existing foundation: a flash-optimised Tectonic behind a FUSE API. That reuses proven durability, tooling and operations, adding a hardware tier rather than a new system.

mcq.q: In Meta's 2024 GenAI clusters, what served checkpoints and data loading?
options: A flash-optimised Tectonic behind a FUSE API
A Hammerspace parallel NFS
Haystack's packed photo files
A new AI-only object store
mcq.why: Checkpoints and data loading used flash-optimised Tectonic via FUSE; the Hammerspace NFS served interactive work.

hook: In December 2023, Meta's servers kept storing Messenger chats but lost the ability to search them. Why?
title: Default E2EE: Messenger's servers store what they can't read
body: Search, indexing and spam checks all assume the server can read what it stores. In December 2023, **end-to-end encryption** became the default on Messenger. The server now stores **ciphertext** it cannot read, because only the users' devices hold the keys. So server-side search and indexing of message content are no longer possible. A privacy decision rewrote what the storage layer is able to do.
takeaway: Once the server cannot read the data, it cannot index it either.
deeper:
**At rest vs end-to-end:** With encryption at rest, the provider's servers can still use keys to decrypt and process data. With end-to-end encryption, only the endpoints hold keys, so the server handles opaque bytes.

**What moves to the client:** In general, features that used to run over stored plaintext, like searching message history, must run on the user's device, over the messages it can decrypt.

**The same line at Apple:** Advanced Data Protection (2022) lets users end-to-end encrypt most iCloud data categories, so Apple does not hold the keys.

**The industry split:** Encryption at rest is now a default at AWS S3, Azure Storage and Google Cloud. End-to-end encryption goes further and changes what the server can do with stored data.

**Design question:** Before promising end-to-end encryption, list every server feature that reads content. Each one must move to the client or go away.

quiz.q: Product wants server-side full-text search over Messenger history after default E2EE. Why can't storage deliver it, and where could search live instead?
quiz.a: The server stores only ciphertext it cannot decrypt, so it cannot build a content index. Search would have to run on the user's device, over messages it can decrypt.

mcq.q: What storage capability did default E2EE on Messenger remove?
options: Server-side search and indexing of message content
Storing messages durably on servers
Replicating messages across data centers
Encrypting messages at rest on disk
mcq.why: With end-to-end encryption the server stores ciphertext it cannot read, so it cannot search or index message content.

hook: Azure doesn't grow its storage by making clusters bigger. What unit does it add instead?
title: Azure grows storage by adding fixed-size stamps
body: One giant cluster makes every failure and every capacity plan giant too. **Windows Azure Storage** (SOSP 2011) is built from **storage stamps**: fixed-size units of racks, each with three layers. A front-end takes requests. A partition layer serves tables, blobs, queues and indexes. A stream layer stores append-only extents with LRC erasure coding. Growth means adding stamps, not growing one cluster.
takeaway: Grow by adding units, not by stretching one.
deeper:
**The stack above the stamps:**
1. Managed Disks, built on page blobs.
2. Blob Storage and ADLS Gen2, with a hierarchical namespace.
3. Azure SQL Hyperscale (Socrates) and Cosmos DB.
4. Azure Cache for Redis.
5. A lake of ADLS Gen2 plus Synapse and Fabric; an Archive tier, with Project Silica glass in research.

**Why append-only extents:** Writing only at the end keeps the stream layer simple and makes erasure coding straightforward once an extent is sealed.

**Why three layers:** The front-end handles requests, the partition layer gives each data object a home and an index, and the stream layer stores bytes durably. Each can be reasoned about on its own.

**The foundation:** Azure's foundation is the stream layer in stamps, its counterpart to Colossus at Google or Tectonic at Meta.

quiz.q: Azure needs hundreds of petabytes more capacity. Under the stamp design, what does it do, and what does it avoid?
quiz.a: It adds more stamps, each a fixed-size unit with its own partition and stream layers. It avoids growing one giant cluster, so each failure domain and capacity plan stays bounded.

mcq.q: Which layer inside an Azure storage stamp stores append-only extents with LRC erasure coding?
options: The stream layer
The partition layer
The front-end layer
The location service
mcq.why: The stream layer stores append-only extents with LRC; the partition layer serves tables, blobs, queues and indexes above it.

hook: Rebuilding one lost fragment with Reed-Solomon means reading many others. How did Azure read fewer?
title: LRC repairs a lost fragment by reading fewer fragments
body: Most repairs fix a single lost fragment, yet classic **Reed-Solomon** makes you read many fragments to rebuild one. **Local Reconstruction Codes** (USENIX ATC 2012) repair a single lost fragment by reading fewer fragments. LRC reduced storage overhead compared with triple replication while keeping repair reads low. At Azure's size, a small cut in overhead is a very large saving, and cheaper repairs mean less network and disk traffic on every failure.
takeaway: Optimise for the common failure: one lost fragment, not many.
deeper:
**How local groups work:** In general, LRC splits the data fragments into smaller groups and adds a parity fragment for each group, plus global parities for the whole set. A single lost fragment can be rebuilt from its own small group instead of from the whole stripe.

**Why single failures matter most:** Disks and nodes usually fail one at a time. If the everyday repair is cheap, the fleet spends far less bandwidth on repair overall, while rarer multi-failure cases fall back to the global parities.

**Versus replication:** Triple replication makes repair a simple copy but stores 3× the data. LRC stores far less while keeping repair reads low.

**Why it earns a paper:** At Azure's scale, shaving a fraction off storage overhead is a very large saving, which is why investing in erasure codes pays.

**Ask this:** What does our most common failure cost to repair, in bytes read?

quiz.q: Two codes have the same storage overhead. Code A rebuilds a lost fragment by reading 12 fragments; code B reads 6. Why might a cloud prefer B despite its complexity?
quiz.a: Single-fragment losses are the most common repair. Reading half as much per repair cuts network and disk traffic on every failure, which is exactly LRC's point.

mcq.q: What does LRC improve on compared with Reed-Solomon?
options: Fewer fragments read to repair one loss
More fragments that can be lost at once
Faster writes for small appends
No need for parity fragments at all
mcq.why: LRC repairs a single lost fragment by reading fewer fragments than Reed-Solomon, with overhead below triple replication.

hook: Azure split SQL Server into three separate services to escape the limits of one machine. Which three?
title: Socrates split SQL Server into compute, log and pages
body: A classic SQL Server keeps compute, log and data pages on one machine, so storage cannot grow past that machine. **Socrates** (SIGMOD 2019), behind Azure SQL Hyperscale, splits SQL Server into compute, a **log service** and page servers over Azure Storage. Around it sit Cosmos DB (GA 2017), a globally distributed multi-model database with five consistency levels; ADLS Gen2 (2019), Blob Storage plus a hierarchical namespace; and Project Silica, research since 2019 into storing data in quartz glass.
takeaway: Split compute from storage, and each grows at its own pace.
deeper:
**Why split the log out:** The log is the ordered record of changes. As its own service, it can be made durable and fast independently of compute, the same instinct as Aurora's "the log is the database".

**What compute gains:** Compute nodes scale on their own, and storage grows past one machine.

**Cosmos DB's angle:** Five consistency levels let applications pick their trade-off between strong guarantees and latency across regions.

**ADLS Gen2's angle:** A real hierarchical namespace makes rename and directory operations atomic and fast, which analytics engines need.

**Silica's angle:** Quartz glass aims at very long archival life, the far end of the archival layer.

**The pattern:** Each system answers one limit: one machine's disk, one consistency model, a flat namespace, media lifetime.

quiz.q: A SQL database's data outgrows its server's disks, but its CPU is fine. How does Socrates' design help, and which part grows?
quiz.a: Socrates separates compute from a log service and page servers over Azure Storage, so page storage grows past one machine without adding compute.

mcq.q: Which pairing is correct?
options: Socrates: compute, log service, page servers
Cosmos DB: quartz glass archival storage
ADLS Gen2: five consistency levels
Project Silica: a namespace for blobs
mcq.why: Socrates splits SQL Server into compute, a log service and page servers. Cosmos DB has five consistency levels; ADLS Gen2 adds the namespace.

hook: Azure deliberately keeps every storage stamp about 30% empty. Why pay for disks you don't fill?
title: Azure keeps each stamp around 70 percent full
body: In 2011, Windows Azure Storage had 70 PB of raw storage in production and was provisioning a few hundred more PB. First-generation stamps held about 2 PB raw; next-generation stamps up to 30 PB. The WAS paper says each stamp is kept around 70 percent utilized. When a stamp nears that level, the **location service** moves accounts to other stamps.

stat.label: target utilization of each Azure stamp

takeaway: Headroom is not waste. It is the room that lets you move.
deeper:
**Why leave headroom:** In general, a unit near full has no room to absorb growth, repairs or bursts of new data. Keeping around 30% free leaves room for all three without an emergency.

**How rebalancing works:** The location service tracks which stamp holds each account. When a stamp nears its ceiling, accounts move to other stamps using inter-stamp replication.

**Growth by counting:** Stamps grew from about 2 PB to up to 30 PB raw. Capacity planning becomes a question of how many stamps to add.

**The honest gap:** Microsoft has not published current exabyte totals for Azure Storage as a single figure. The 70 PB is a 2011 number, useful for design history, not for today's size. Always read a storage figure with its year attached.

quiz.q: Your storage cluster runs at 92% full, and every new customer triggers a scramble. What would Azure's stamp practice change?
quiz.a: Set a utilization ceiling around 70%. When a unit nears it, move accounts to other units or add units, so growth never lands on a nearly full system.

mcq.q: What happens when an Azure stamp nears its utilization ceiling?
options: The location service moves accounts to other stamps
The stamp is expanded with extra racks
New writes are rejected until data is deleted
Data is pushed down to the Archive tier
mcq.why: Stamps are kept around 70 percent utilized; as one nears that level, the location service moves accounts to other stamps.

hook: Microsoft owns LinkedIn and GitHub. Whose storage stack do they run on?
title: Microsoft builds its cloud core, and buys whole companies
body: Microsoft builds its core cloud storage in-house. It also buys companies and products, and some keep their own stacks: it owns LinkedIn and GitHub, which run their own. Azure's defining design choice is the **storage stamp**, a fixed-size unit of racks with its own partition and stream layers. Growth means adding stamps, not growing one giant cluster. So Azure scales as many bounded units, each small enough to plan for and to fail on its own.
takeaway: Scale by adding bounded units, and capacity planning becomes counting.
deeper:
**Build vs buy, both:** Microsoft builds its core and buys companies. Azure Storage, Cosmos DB and Socrates are built. LinkedIn and GitHub arrived by acquisition with their own stacks.

**A public wrinkle:** In 2019 LinkedIn announced a plan to move its data centers to Azure. In 2022 it paused that plan and kept its own data centers, citing the value of its existing on-prem investment.

**What stamps buy:**
1. A small blast radius: a failure stays inside one stamp.
2. Simple capacity planning: count stamps.
3. Rebalancing by moving accounts between stamps.

**What stamps cost:** Capacity can strand across stamps, and accounts must move to rebalance. Meta's giant Tectonic clusters make the opposite trade.

**The cost lever:** Better erasure codes like LRC cut overhead, and at Azure's size a small cut is a large saving.

quiz.q: An Azure-style team debates growing one storage cluster to 200 PB or running seven 30 PB stamps. What does each choice optimize?
quiz.a: Stamps keep each failure domain small and make planning a matter of counting, but strand capacity. One big cluster pools resources better, but a bad failure or deploy reaches more data.

mcq.q: How does Azure grow its storage capacity?
options: By adding more fixed-size stamps
By growing one giant cluster
By buying capacity from other clouds
By moving cold data to Project Silica
mcq.why: Azure's defining choice is the stamp: growth means adding stamps, each with its own partition and stream layers.

hook: How big should one storage failure domain be? Azure and Meta gave opposite answers. Who was right?
title: Stamps or giant clusters: outage scope vs wasted capacity
body: Azure's stamps and Meta's exabyte clusters are opposite answers to one question: how big should one storage **failure domain** be? Stamps keep the blast radius small and turn capacity planning into counting stamps. Giant clusters reduce **stranded capacity**, because more tenants share the same pool. Neither is universally right. The deciding question is which cost dominates for you: the scope of an outage, or the capacity you waste.
takeaway: Size your failure domain by the cost you fear more.
deeper:
**What stamps trade away:** Capacity can strand across stamps: one stamp may have free space while another is near its ceiling. Rebalancing needs account moves between stamps.

**What giant clusters trade away:** Resources pool better, but a bad failure or bad deploy can affect more data at once.

**How to decide:**
1. If an outage touching everyone would be unacceptable, favour smaller units.
2. If hardware cost dominates and workloads complement each other, favour bigger pools.
3. Either way, measure both costs rather than arguing taste.

**Mitigations exist on both sides:** Stamps rebalance by moving accounts with inter-stamp replication. Big systems can still limit how much a single failure touches, the way AWS splits services into cells.

**Ask this:** Which hurts us more this year: a wider outage, or a bigger hardware bill?

quiz.q: A payments company with strict uptime promises and modest data volume must choose between stamps and one giant cluster. Which fits, and why?
quiz.a: Stamps. Its dominant cost is outage scope, not wasted capacity, so small, bounded failure domains matter more than the pooling gains of a giant cluster.

mcq.q: What does Azure's stamp design trade away compared with Meta's giant clusters?
options: Pooling efficiency: capacity can strand across stamps
Blast-radius control during failures
Simple capacity planning
Erasure coding inside a stamp
mcq.why: Stamps limit blast radius and simplify planning, but capacity can strand across stamps and accounts must move to rebalance.

hook: Analytics needs atomic folder renames. Blob storage lacked them. How did Azure add them without a new system?
title: ADLS Gen2 added real folders to blobs, not a new system
body: Object stores usually fake folders with name prefixes, so renaming a directory means touching every object under it, one by one. Analytics jobs rename directories constantly. Microsoft's answer was **ADLS Gen2** (2019): add a real **hierarchical namespace** to Blob Storage instead of running a separate file system. Users kept one storage account, and the namespace made rename and directory operations atomic and fast. It is migration by adding a capability to the existing system.
takeaway: Before building beside a system, ask whether you can build into it.
deeper:
**Why renames matter to analytics:** Jobs often write output to a temporary directory and rename it into place when done, so readers never see half-written results. On a flat namespace that rename is many operations and not atomic; with a real namespace it is one.

**Why not a separate file system:** Two systems mean two copies of data, two access models and a pipeline to keep them in sync. Adding the namespace to Blob Storage kept one account and one copy.

**The pattern:** It resembles S3's move to strong consistency. Both upgraded a system customers already used instead of launching a parallel product.

**Where it sits:** ADLS Gen2 plus Synapse and Fabric form Azure's lake layer, on top of the stamp-based storage foundation.

quiz.q: A Spark job writes results to a temp folder, then renames it into place. Why is that risky on a flat object store, and how does ADLS Gen2 change it?
quiz.a: On a flat store the rename is many per-object operations, so readers may see partial results. ADLS Gen2's hierarchical namespace makes the directory rename atomic and fast.

mcq.q: What did ADLS Gen2 add to Azure Blob Storage?
options: A real hierarchical namespace
A separate analytics file system
Strong read-after-write consistency
Local Reconstruction Codes
mcq.why: ADLS Gen2 added a hierarchical namespace to Blob Storage, making rename and directory operations atomic and fast in one account.

hook: Most cloud security settings have an off switch. Which Azure Storage protection has none?
title: Azure's encryption at rest has no off switch
body: A default setting can still be switched off by mistake. Azure Storage encrypts all data at rest by default with **256-bit AES**, and it cannot be turned off. Customers can bring their own keys. For residency, Microsoft's **EU Data Boundary** is a commitment to store and process EU customer data within the EU for its core cloud services, and Microsoft has published documentation on the boundary.
takeaway: The safest default is one nobody is allowed to change.
deeper:
**Default vs mandatory:** S3 encrypts new objects by default since January 2023, and Google Cloud encrypts all customer data at rest by default. Azure's wording goes a step further: its encryption at rest cannot be turned off.

**What customer keys add:** Bringing your own key gives you control over rotation and revocation, even though Microsoft runs the storage.

**Storage and processing:** The EU commitment covers both storing and processing EU customer data in the EU, for core cloud services. Storing data in the EU while processing it elsewhere would not meet that promise.

**What encryption at rest does not do:** The provider's servers can still use keys to decrypt and process data. End-to-end encryption, like Messenger's default, is a different promise.

**Ask this:** For each compliance claim, is it a default, a mandatory control or a commitment? They carry different weight.

quiz.q: An auditor asks whether an admin could disable encryption at rest on any Azure Storage account. What is the answer?
quiz.a: No. Azure Storage encrypts all data at rest with 256-bit AES by default and it cannot be turned off; customers can only choose to bring their own keys.

mcq.q: What distinguishes Azure Storage's encryption at rest?
options: It cannot be turned off
It covers only objects written since 2023
It requires customer-managed keys
It is end-to-end, so Microsoft can't read data
mcq.why: Azure encrypts all data at rest with 256-bit AES by default, and it cannot be disabled; customer keys are optional.

hook: Uber runs exabytes of storage, yet much of its stack is thin layers of its own code. Thin on top of what?
title: Uber's stack: thin custom layers on MySQL and HDFS
body: Writing a durable storage engine is slow and risky, so Uber mostly doesn't. Its operational data lives in **Docstore**, which evolved from Schemaless (2016) and runs MySQL on each node. Redis caches, called CacheFront, sit in front of Docstore, and Cassandra runs alongside. Analytics runs on HDFS, over 1 EB per region, with **Apache Hudi** tables and Hive, Presto and Spark on top. The hardware started in Uber's own data centers and is moving to Oracle Cloud and Google Cloud.
takeaway: Borrow the hard part. Build the part that makes it yours.
deeper:
**The stack, bottom up:**
1. On-prem data centers, moving to Oracle Cloud and Google Cloud.
2. A MySQL fleet, Cassandra, and HDFS moving to Google Cloud Storage.
3. Schemaless, evolved into Docstore, on MySQL.
4. Redis caches (CacheFront) in front of Docstore.
5. A lake of Hudi tables with Hive, Presto and Spark; colder data in cheaper storage.

**An early engine choice:** In 2016 Uber moved core storage from Postgres to MySQL, citing write amplification and replication issues. MySQL then became the base for Schemaless and Docstore.

**Where the effort goes:** Uber's code handles sharding, replication and APIs. The durable single-node engine stays in well-tested open source.

**Direction of travel:** Since 2023 Uber has moved toward public cloud, and the lake is moving to Google Cloud.

quiz.q: Why would Uber build Docstore on MySQL instead of writing its own storage engine?
quiz.a: It keeps the hard part, a durable single-node engine, in well-tested code and puts Uber's effort into sharding, replication and APIs, where its needs actually differ.

mcq.q: What sits in front of Docstore at Uber?
options: Redis caches called CacheFront
Memcache and TAO
EVCache
Couchbase
mcq.why: Uber runs Redis caches (CacheFront) in front of Docstore. TAO is Meta's, EVCache is Netflix's, Couchbase is LinkedIn's.

hook: Uber's lake rewrote whole tables every day just to apply a few changes. What did it build to stop that?
title: Hudi: write only the changed records, not whole tables
body: Plain files on HDFS cannot be updated in place, so applying a day's changes used to mean rewriting whole tables. Most rows had not changed, so most of that work was waste. In 2016 and 2017 Uber created **Apache Hudi** to bring **upserts** and **incremental reads** to HDFS. Jobs write only the changed records, and downstream jobs read only what changed since their last run. Hudi is now an Apache project.
takeaway: Process the change, not the whole table.
deeper:
**Upserts:** An upsert inserts a record if it is new and updates it if it exists. Hudi tracks which files hold which keys, so it can apply updates without rewriting the full dataset.

**Incremental reads:** Instead of re-scanning a whole table each run, a downstream job asks for records changed since a point in time. Pipelines chain small deltas instead of full reloads.

**Where it sits:** Hudi is a thin layer on HDFS and Parquet, the same pattern as Docstore on MySQL: Uber builds the layer and borrows the engine.

**Why it matters at Uber's size:** Uber's Hadoop held more than 1 exabyte across tens of thousands of servers in each of two regions in 2024. Rewriting whole tables daily at that size would burn enormous compute and I/O.

**A cousin:** Netflix created Iceberg for a related problem on object storage: slow listing and no safe concurrent writes.

quiz.q: A daily job rewrites a 50 TB table to apply 20 GB of changed rows. What would Hudi change, and what do downstream jobs gain?
quiz.a: Upsert only the changed records instead of rewriting 50 TB. Downstream jobs use incremental reads to fetch just what changed since their last run.

mcq.q: Which two capabilities did Uber build Hudi to add on HDFS?
options: Upserts and incremental reads
Cross-table transactions and strong consistency
Erasure coding and automatic tiering
Streaming ingestion and in-memory caching
mcq.why: Uber created Hudi for upserts and incremental reads on HDFS, so jobs write and read only changed records.

hook: Uber's Hadoop holds more than an exabyte. Is that the company total, or something else?
title: Uber: over 1 EB of Hadoop in each of two regions
body: Uber publishes two headline figures. Docstore, per a 2020 blog, serves tens of millions of queries per second with 99.99 percent or more availability, over tens of petabytes of operational data. Hadoop, per a 2024 post, holds more than 1 exabyte across tens of thousands of servers in **each** of two regions. That second number is per region, and it is **batch** data, not the online database.

stat.label: Uber Hadoop data in each of two regions

takeaway: Read the scope before the size: per region, per cluster or total.
deeper:
**Two worlds, two numbers:** Docstore is operational: small records, many queries per second, strict availability. Hadoop is analytical: huge files scanned in bulk. Tens of petabytes against over an exabyte per region shows how much bigger analytics data grows than the online store.

**Why the dates matter:** The Docstore figure is from 2020 and the Hadoop figure from 2024. They describe different moments of systems that keep growing.

**Where the exabytes are going:** Uber's 2024 data platform post says batch analytics and ML data are moving from on-prem Hadoop to Google Cloud. Moving more than an exabyte per region is why Uber moved bytes first and changed engines later.

**Compare carefully:** LinkedIn's HDFS held over 1 EB in total in 2021. Uber's figure is per region, so the two numbers do not describe the same scope.

quiz.q: Someone says Uber and LinkedIn both run "about an exabyte of Hadoop." What detail does that miss?
quiz.a: Scope and year. Uber's 2024 figure is over 1 EB in each of two regions; LinkedIn's 2021 figure is over 1 EB in total across its clusters.

mcq.q: What availability did Uber report for Docstore in 2020?
options: 99.99 percent or more
99.9 percent
99 percent
99.95 percent
mcq.why: Uber's 2020 Docstore blog reported tens of millions of QPS, 99.99 percent or more availability and tens of petabytes of data.

hook: Uber's Docstore serves tens of millions of queries a second. Uber didn't write its storage engine. How?
title: Uber builds thin layers on proven engines
body: The riskiest code in a database is the durable single-node engine, the part that must never lose a write. Uber keeps that part in well-tested open source. Schemaless and Docstore sit on **MySQL**; Hudi sits on HDFS and Parquet. Uber's own effort goes into sharding, replication and APIs. Historically it built on open source in its own data centers; since 2023 it has moved toward public cloud, with Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Google Cloud as partners.
takeaway: Let the engine be boring. Make the layer above it yours.
deeper:
**What a thin layer adds:** What the business needs on top of an engine that already works: partitioning across many nodes, replication across zones, a document API, change capture. The engine handles durability on each node.

**Why it works:** Engines like MySQL carry years of production hardening. Rebuilding that from scratch would take years and bring new bugs into the one place bugs cost the most.

**The Docstore example:** MySQL on each node, Raft replication, strict serializability per partition, and partitions of 3 to 5 nodes spread across zones.

**The range:** Google and Meta build down to the file system. Dropbox built its own block store. Uber sits at the thin end of that range.

**The cloud shift:** Uber's 2024 data platform post says its lake is moving to Google Cloud.

quiz.q: Your team wants a new document database. One camp proposes a custom storage engine, the other a layer over MySQL. Which does Uber's approach favour, and why?
quiz.a: A layer over MySQL. It keeps the durable single-node engine in well-tested code and spends effort on sharding, replication and APIs, where the team's needs actually differ.

mcq.q: In Uber's approach, which part stays in well-tested open source?
options: The durable single-node storage engine
The sharding and routing logic
The replication across zones
The document API that teams call
mcq.why: Uber writes thin layers for sharding, replication and APIs on proven engines like MySQL, keeping the durable engine in tested code.

hook: A team needs to look up Uber data by a second key. Normally that means building a pipeline. Why not at Uber?
title: Docstore: small partitions plus built-in views
body: Every team that needs a second access path usually builds its own pipeline, and each pipeline can drift or break. **Docstore**, described in 2020, builds that in. Data is split into partitions of 3 to 5 nodes spread across zones, with MySQL on each node, **Raft** replication and strict serializability per partition. **Materialized views** and change data capture inside Docstore let teams read data by a second key without building their own pipelines.
takeaway: Build the second index once, in the platform, not in every team.
deeper:
**Why partitions of 3 to 5 nodes:** Each partition is a small Raft group. A majority must agree on each write, so a partition survives losing a minority of its nodes. Spreading nodes across zones means one zone failing does not take a partition down.

**Why per-partition serializability:** Strict serializability within a partition gives strong guarantees where most operations happen, without global coordination on every write.

**What views and CDC replace:** Without them, a team wanting a second key would read a change stream, transform it and write to another store, and own that pipeline's correctness. Docstore does it for them.

**The contrast:** Pinterest built secondary indexes in application code without transactions, and index and data drifted apart. Moving that job into the platform is one way to avoid that class of bug.

**The scale:** Tens of millions of queries per second over tens of petabytes (2020).

quiz.q: A Docstore partition has 5 nodes spread across three zones. One zone fails, taking 2 nodes with it. Can the partition still accept writes?
quiz.a: Yes. Raft needs a majority, 3 of 5, to commit a write, and 3 nodes remain in the other zones.

mcq.q: What lets Docstore users read data by a second key without their own pipelines?
options: Materialized views and change data capture
Application-level secondary indexes
A nightly export to Hadoop
Redis caches in CacheFront
mcq.why: Docstore offers materialized views and CDC inside the database, so teams don't build their own pipelines for second-key reads.

hook: Uber had to move over an exabyte of analytics data to Google Cloud without breaking jobs. What went first?
title: Uber moved an exabyte by moving the bytes first
body: Moving an exabyte while thousands of jobs keep running punishes any big-bang step. Uber's 2024 plan went in four steps. Data moved to Google Cloud Storage while the existing Hadoop stack ran on cloud VMs, and a **cloud storage connector** gave HDFS compatibility, so jobs did not change. **Data access proxies** routed each read to on-prem or cloud. HiveSync replicated in both directions. Only then came managed services like Dataproc and BigQuery.
takeaway: Move the bytes, keep the software. Modernize once the dust settles.
deeper:
**The four steps:**
1. Move bytes, keep the software: data to Google Cloud Storage, Hadoop on cloud VMs, an HDFS-compatible connector so jobs run unchanged.
2. Federate access: proxies route each read to on-prem or cloud, so users need not know where a dataset lives today.
3. Replicate in both directions during the transition, with HiveSync.
4. Only then modernize to Dataproc and BigQuery.

**Why this order:** Each step changes one thing, so each can be rolled back on its own. If a job breaks after step 1, the cause is the storage location, not a new engine.

**What the proxies buy:** Datasets can move one at a time with no flag day, because readers ask the proxy, not a hard-coded location.

**The scale at stake:** More than 1 exabyte in each of two regions (2024).

quiz.q: Halfway through Uber's migration, some jobs slow down. Under its plan, how do you narrow the cause and back out?
quiz.a: Only the storage location has changed so far, behind an HDFS-compatible connector, so look there. Proxies and two-way replication let you route those datasets back on-prem.

mcq.q: What let Uber's existing Hadoop jobs run unchanged against Google Cloud Storage?
options: A cloud storage connector with HDFS compatibility
Rewriting every job for BigQuery first
Copying data back to HDFS every night
Running all jobs on-prem during the move
mcq.why: A cloud storage connector gave HDFS compatibility, so jobs kept working while their bytes moved to Google Cloud Storage.

hook: Uber's cloud migration had an obvious shortcut: move the data and switch engines in one go. Why skip it?
title: Never change storage and engines at the same time
body: Uber did not change the storage system and the compute engines at the same time. It is the rule of a controlled experiment, applied to infrastructure. Change one variable, and when something breaks you know which change did it and can undo just that. Change two, and every failure has two suspects. Changing one variable at a time makes each step **reversible**. This is **lift, then shift**: move first, modernize second.
takeaway: One variable per step. Two suspects per failure is one too many.
deeper:
**How the analogy maps:** In an experiment, you change one input so any difference in the result has one cause. In a migration, the storage location and the engine are the inputs; job failures and slowdowns are the results.

**Uber's sequence:**
1. Storage moves to Google Cloud Storage; Hadoop engines stay.
2. Proxies and HiveSync keep both sides usable.
3. Engines move to Dataproc and BigQuery later.

**The same rule elsewhere:** Meta ran MyRocks as replicas beside InnoDB before promoting it. Dropbox dark-launched Magic Pocket in August 2014 and had moved over 90 percent of user data off S3 by October 2015.

**The cost:** Two-phase moves take longer and mean running old and new side by side. That is the price of being able to back out.

**Ask this:** If this step fails at 2 a.m., can we undo exactly this step and nothing else?

quiz.q: A team proposes moving its warehouse to a new cloud and switching from Hive to a new query engine in the same quarter. What is your objection, and the alternative?
quiz.a: Two changes at once make failures ambiguous and rollback hard. Move storage first behind a compatible interface, keep the engine, then switch engines as a separate, reversible step.

mcq.q: Why does changing one variable at a time make a migration safer?
options: Each step can be rolled back on its own
It moves the data faster overall
It avoids running two systems at once
It removes the need for testing
mcq.why: With one change per step, a failure has one suspect, and each step can be undone independently.

hook: Netflix runs no traditional data centers for its services, yet puts its own hardware inside ISPs. Why?
title: Netflix: AWS for everything, plus its own video CDN
body: Netflix moved its streaming service and data to AWS between 2008 and January 2016, and runs no traditional data centers for its services. But one kind of byte is special. Video must sit close to viewers, so Netflix built **Open Connect** (2012), its own CDN appliances placed inside ISPs. Inside AWS, **Cassandra** is the main online store, EVCache caches across regions, S3 holds video masters and warehouse files, and Iceberg tables organise the lake.
takeaway: Rent everything ordinary. Own the one thing your product is.
deeper:
**The stack:**
1. AWS, plus Open Connect appliances in ISPs.
2. S3 for video masters and warehouse files; Open Connect for video bytes near users.
3. Cassandra, the main online store; EVCache, memcached-based and cross-region.
4. A data abstraction layer: KV and TimeSeries services.
5. A lake of Iceberg tables with Spark and Trino; archival in S3 colder classes.

**Why Cassandra:** It was chosen, from about 2010, for multi-region, always-writable replication.

**Heavy bytes apart:** Video lives on Open Connect and in S3. Online databases hold only metadata and user state.

**What's not published:** Netflix publishes design detail more than totals. No single verified figure for its warehouse or Cassandra fleet is available here, so none is given. Treat any confident Netflix byte count with suspicion.

quiz.q: Netflix buys almost all its infrastructure from AWS. Why build Open Connect instead of using a generic CDN?
quiz.a: Video delivery is the core product, and the bytes must sit inside ISPs close to viewers. Netflix builds only what makes its product special and buys the rest.

mcq.q: Where do Netflix's online databases fit relative to video bytes?
options: They hold metadata and user state; video lives elsewhere
They store the video masters used for streaming
They cache video segments for ISPs
They replace S3 for the data warehouse
mcq.why: Netflix separates heavy bytes: video on Open Connect and S3, while Cassandra and friends hold only metadata and user state.

hook: Netflix buys its compute and storage from AWS but refuses to buy one thing. What, and why?
title: Netflix buys the cloud and builds only its special part
body: Most companies should not build infrastructure that is not their product. Netflix is the leading example of "cloud for everything except the one thing that is special". It buys compute and storage from AWS and runs no traditional data centers for its services. But video delivery is the core product, so it builds its own CDN, **Open Connect**, placing bytes inside ISPs close to viewers. Inside AWS it still builds platform layers: Cassandra tooling, EVCache, Iceberg and a **data abstraction layer**.
takeaway: Build where you differ. Buy where you don't.
deeper:
**Why the CDN is the exception:** Streaming quality depends on how close the bytes sit to the viewer. That is the product itself, so owning it pays.

**Why build on top of AWS anyway:** Buying infrastructure does not remove platform work. Netflix built Cassandra operations tooling, EVCache (open-sourced 2013), Iceberg (Apache 2018) and, recently, a KV abstraction layer.

**The first axis:** Is storage your product? AWS, Azure and Google Cloud sell storage, so they must build it. Dropbox's product is file storage, so it rebuilt it. Netflix's product is video, so it built the part that serves video and bought the rest.

**In four words:** Buy infra, build platform.

**Ask this:** Which of our infrastructure is the product, and which is plumbing someone else runs better?

quiz.q: A streaming startup considers building its own object store to save money. By Netflix's rule, what should it build first, if anything?
quiz.a: Only what makes its product special, likely delivery close to viewers. Object storage is not its product, so buying it from a cloud fits Netflix's pattern.

mcq.q: Why does Netflix build Open Connect rather than buy CDN capacity?
options: Video delivery is its core product
AWS offers no storage service
Open Connect is cheaper than S3 for masters
Regulators require ISP-hosted video
mcq.why: Netflix buys the rest from AWS but builds the CDN because video delivery is the product, and the bytes must sit inside ISPs.

hook: At Netflix, moving one dataset off Cassandra could touch a hundred teams. How did it become one team's job?
title: Netflix's KV layer turns migrations into a platform task
body: When every application talks to its database directly, changing that database means changing every application. Netflix's **KV Data Abstraction Layer**, described in 2024, puts one key-value API in front of Cassandra, EVCache and other backends. Behind it, the platform team can change the storage engine, tune caching, and handle large values and pagination without every team rewriting code. "Move this dataset from Cassandra" becomes a platform task, not a hundred-team project.
takeaway: An abstraction layer is a down payment on every future migration.
deeper:
**The cost:** One more network hop of latency, and a platform team to build and run the layer. Neither is free.

**When it pays:** At Netflix's size, with many teams on shared storage, the trade is clearly worth it. At a 20-engineer startup it is not: few teams, few migrations, and the hop and the team cost more than they save.

**What the platform can do behind the API:**
1. Swap or add storage engines.
2. Tune caching with EVCache.
3. Handle large values and pagination once, for everyone.

**The third axis:** When hundreds of teams use storage, a shared foundation plus an abstraction layer beats one-off choices. When a handful do, polyglot by team is fine.

**A sibling:** Uber's HDFS-compatible cloud connector also hid where bytes live, which is what made its GCP move cheap.

quiz.q: A 20-engineer startup wants to copy Netflix's KV abstraction layer in front of its one Postgres database. What would you advise?
quiz.a: Skip it for now. The layer costs an extra hop and a team to run it; with few teams and rare migrations, those costs outweigh the benefit Netflix gets at scale.

mcq.q: What does Netflix's KV abstraction layer cost?
options: An extra network hop and a platform team
Every team rewriting its data access code
Losing Cassandra's multi-region replication
A second full copy of all data
mcq.why: One stable API makes backend changes cheap, at the price of an extra hop of latency and a team to run the layer.

hook: Any Netflix region can serve any user. What must be true of its databases for that to work?
title: Netflix scales with active-active regions and Iceberg on S3
body: If only one region can take writes, losing it stops the service. Netflix runs **multi-region active-active**: Cassandra and EVCache replicate across AWS regions, so any region can serve any user. Heavy bytes stay out of the databases: video lives on Open Connect and in S3, while online stores hold only metadata and user state. For analytics, **Iceberg** tables on S3 replaced the older Hive layout, which had slow directory listing and no safe concurrent writes.
takeaway: Keep databases small by keeping the heavy bytes out of them.
deeper:
**Why Cassandra fits active-active:** It was chosen for multi-region, always-writable replication. Each region accepts writes and replicates to the others.

**Why EVCache replicates too:** A cache that lived in only one region would leave other regions cold after a failover. Cross-region replication keeps caches warm everywhere.

**Why separate heavy bytes:** Video files are huge and immutable. Online databases stay small and fast when they hold only metadata and user state.

**Why Hive tables hurt on object storage:** Hive found a table's files by listing directories, which is slow on object storage at scale, and it had no safe way for two writers to commit at once. Iceberg tracks files in its own metadata, so readers skip listing and writers commit safely.

**The trade:** Active-active accepts cross-region replication lag in exchange for surviving the loss of a region.

quiz.q: An analytics team on S3 sees queries spend minutes listing partitions, and two jobs writing one table corrupt it. What did Netflix build for this, and how does it help?
quiz.a: Iceberg. It tracks table files in its own metadata instead of listing directories, and supports safe concurrent commits, the two problems the Hive layout had on object storage.

mcq.q: Why did Netflix build Iceberg to replace Hive tables on S3?
options: Slow directory listing and no safe concurrent writes
Hive could not store columnar files
S3 lacked the consistency Iceberg needs
Hive tables only worked on on-prem HDFS
mcq.why: The Hive layout on object storage had slow directory listing and no safe concurrent writes; Iceberg was built to fix both.

hook: Netflix's move to the cloud took far longer than a typical migration. Why so long?
title: Netflix took seven years to move to AWS, and rebuilt
body: Lifting systems into a cloud unchanged is fast, but it carries data-center assumptions along. Netflix moved its streaming service and data from its own data centers to AWS between 2008 and January 2016, about seven years, and rebuilt most of its systems as **cloud-native** services instead of lifting them unchanged. Later, moving Hive tables to **Iceberg** made future layout changes cheap: an Iceberg table can change its partitioning without rewriting data, so a layout change becomes a metadata operation.
takeaway: Some migrations pay once. Good formats pay again on every later change.
deeper:
**Why rebuild instead of lift:** Cloud-native services assume machines can vanish and capacity can grow on demand. Code built for a data center often assumes the opposite. Rebuilding took longer but produced systems that fit the cloud.

**Contrast with Uber:** Uber's GCP move deliberately lifted first, keeping Hadoop and moving bytes, then modernized later. Netflix rebuilt as it went. Uber's order keeps each step reversible; Netflix's avoids carrying old designs forward.

**How Iceberg changes partitioning:** Partitioning is recorded in table metadata. Change the scheme and new data follows it, while old data stays readable under the old one. No rewrite is needed.

**Why that matters:** Rewriting a huge table to change its layout is itself a migration. Making it a metadata operation removes a whole class of future projects.

quiz.q: Your analytics table is partitioned by day, and queries now need hourly partitions. With Hive you would rewrite petabytes. What changes with Iceberg?
quiz.a: Iceberg lets the table change its partitioning without rewriting data. New data uses hourly partitions and old data stays as is, so the change is a metadata operation.

mcq.q: How did Netflix approach its move to AWS?
options: It rebuilt most systems as cloud-native services
It lifted every system unchanged in one year
It kept its data centers for all storage
It moved analytics only and kept streaming on-prem
mcq.why: Over about seven years, Netflix rebuilt most of its systems as cloud-native services rather than lifting them unchanged.

predict.q: Roughly how long did Netflix's move from its own data centers to AWS take?
options: About seven years
About one year
About three years

hook: LinkedIn wrote most of its own storage stack and open-sourced much of it. What does each piece hold?
title: LinkedIn's stack: Kafka, Espresso, Venice, Ambry, HDFS
body: LinkedIn builds heavily and open-sources much of it. **Kafka** (2011), the distributed log LinkedIn created, is its data-movement backbone. **Espresso** (SIGMOD 2013), a timeline-consistent document store on sharded MySQL with change capture, holds primary data. **Venice**, in production since the end of 2016, serves derived data fed by batch pushes and streams. Ambry (SIGMOD 2016) stores media blobs. HDFS held over 1 EB in 2021, with Spark, Trino and Iceberg on top.
takeaway: Give each kind of data its own home, and a log to move between them.
deeper:
**The stack:**
1. LinkedIn's own data centers.
2. HDFS (over 1 EB, 2021), Ambry for media, Espresso on MySQL.
3. Couchbase and in-process caches.
4. Venice for derived key-value data; Kafka moving data between systems.
5. A lake of Spark, Trino and Iceberg with the OpenHouse control plane.

**Why Kafka sits in the middle:** Derived data is computed from primary data and pushed back out for serving. A durable log is a natural pipe for that movement.

**Voldemort's legacy:** LinkedIn's early Dynamo-style key-value store, from about 2009, was later replaced by Venice for read-only data.

**Open source:** Kafka, Venice, Ambry and Voldemort are all open source.

**What's not published:** LinkedIn's archival layer has no published design, so it is left blank rather than guessed.

quiz.q: A member edits their profile, and hours later their recommendations change. Which LinkedIn systems likely handled each step?
quiz.a: Espresso stored the edit as primary data. Hadoop or Spark computed new recommendations from it, and Venice served the result as derived data, with Kafka moving data between systems.

mcq.q: Which LinkedIn system is the source of truth for primary data such as profile edits?
options: Espresso
Venice
Ambry
Voldemort
mcq.why: Primary data goes to Espresso. Venice serves derived data, Ambry stores media blobs, and Voldemort was the early key-value store.

hook: LinkedIn's derived-data store takes in over three trillion rows a day. Why so much for read-only data?
title: Venice ingests 1.2 PB and 3 trillion rows a day
body: Derived data, like recommendations and ML features, is recomputed constantly and pushed in bulk, so its store must absorb huge volumes. In 2022 **Venice** had 1,800 datasets, over 300 applications, and 17 production clusters per region across 4,000 physical hosts. It ingested 1.2 PB and over three trillion rows per day, and peaked at 45 million **batch-get** key lookups per second.
takeaway: Read-only for users can still mean write-heavy for storage.
deeper:
**Why ingest is so large:** Derived datasets are rebuilt from primary data by offline jobs and pushed as whole new versions, alongside streaming updates. Every refresh rewrites large amounts of data, even though applications only read it.

**Batch-get lookups:** A batch-get fetches many keys in one request, useful when a page needs many values at once. 45 million per second is the published peak.

**HDFS alongside:** LinkedIn reported in 2021 that its Hadoop clusters together store over 1 exabyte, with the largest cluster around 10,000 nodes.

**Read the units:** 1.2 PB per day is ingest volume, 45 million per second is lookup rate, 4,000 is hosts. Different quantities, one system.

**Scope:** The 17 clusters are per region, not a total.

quiz.q: Venice data is read-only for applications. Why does it still ingest 1.2 PB a day?
quiz.a: Derived datasets are recomputed offline and pushed as whole new versions, plus streaming updates, so storage absorbs massive writes even though applications only read.

mcq.q: In 2022, how many production Venice clusters did LinkedIn run per region?
mcq.why: Venice ran 17 production clusters per region across 4,000 physical hosts, serving 1,800 datasets for over 300 applications.

hook: LinkedIn keeps a member's profile edits and their "People You May Know" scores in different systems. Why?
title: Guard primary data. Rebuild derived data.
body: Treating all data alike means overprotecting what can be rebuilt or underprotecting what cannot. LinkedIn splits them. **Primary data**, like profile edits and messages, goes to Espresso, the source of truth. **Derived data**, like recommendations, "People You May Know" scores and ML features, is computed in Hadoop or Spark and pushed into Venice for fast read-only serving. Derived data can be rebuilt from primary data, so it needs less durability and can be bulk-loaded.
takeaway: Ask of every dataset: if we lost it, could we recompute it?
deeper:
**Why primary data gets the care:** It cannot be rebuilt. Lose a message and it is gone. So it gets careful replication and change capture.

**Why derived data can be cheaper:** If a Venice dataset is lost or corrupted, the offline job that produced it can run again. That allows lower durability, bulk loading and wholesale replacement.

**How Venice serves it:** Offline jobs push whole new versions of a dataset, and Venice swaps versions atomically. Reads never see a half-loaded dataset.

**The general rule:** Classify each dataset by whether it can be recomputed. The answer shapes replication, backup, the write path and how you migrate it.

**A caution:** Rebuilding still costs compute and time. Derived data can have lower durability, not none, if the product cannot wait for a recompute.

quiz.q: Your team stores ML features in the same triple-replicated, backed-up database as user payments. What would LinkedIn's split suggest?
quiz.a: Features are derived data, rebuildable from primary data. Serve them from a bulk-loaded, version-swapped store with lower durability, and keep careful replication for payments.

mcq.q: Why can LinkedIn's derived data live with lower durability than primary data?
options: It can be rebuilt from primary data
Applications never read it
It is smaller than primary data
It is stored only in caches
mcq.why: Derived data is computed from primary data, so it can be recomputed if lost. Primary data cannot.

hook: In 2019, LinkedIn, owned by Microsoft, announced a move to Microsoft's cloud. What happened by 2022?
title: LinkedIn planned a move to Azure, then shelved it
body: Owning a cloud does not mean every acquired company moves onto it. In 2019 LinkedIn announced a plan to move its data centers to Azure. In 2022 it paused that plan and kept its own data centers, citing the value of its existing **on-prem investment**. It is a public example of a large company deciding that a full **cloud move** was not worth it at that time, even with its parent company's cloud on offer.
takeaway: "Move to the cloud" is a decision to re-make, not a direction to obey.
deeper:
**Why it is notable:** Microsoft owns LinkedIn and runs Azure. If any company had a reason to move, LinkedIn did. Pausing suggests the decision turned on LinkedIn's own situation, not on who owns whom.

**The stated reason:** The value of the existing on-prem investment. LinkedIn already operated data centers and a large storage estate, including HDFS clusters holding over 1 exabyte in 2021.

**The opposite direction:** Uber has moved toward public cloud since 2023, with Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Google Cloud as partners, and its lake is moving to Google Cloud.

**Time matters:** The same question can get different answers at different companies and at different times. LinkedIn's call was about that time, not forever.

**Ask this:** What have we already paid for, and what would a move actually save?

quiz.q: An executive says, "We're owned by a cloud provider, so we must migrate to its cloud." Which public case pushes back?
quiz.a: LinkedIn. Owned by Microsoft, it announced an Azure move in 2019 but paused it in 2022, citing the value of its existing on-prem investment.

mcq.q: Why did LinkedIn pause its planned Azure move in 2022?
options: The value of its existing on-prem investment
Azure could not hold an exabyte of data
Regulators blocked the migration
Kafka could not run on Azure
mcq.why: LinkedIn kept its own data centers, citing the value of its existing on-prem investment.

hook: LinkedIn pushes whole new dataset versions while apps read them. Why do readers never see one half-loaded?
title: Venice swaps whole dataset versions atomically
body: Loading a new dataset into a live store row by row means readers see a mix of old and new. **Venice** avoids that with **push-based serving**: offline jobs push a whole new version of a dataset, and Venice swaps versions atomically. Reads never see a half-loaded dataset. HDFS shows a different pressure: LinkedIn's 2021 post describes a lot of work to keep a single **NameNode** healthy at very large object counts, the classic HDFS metadata bottleneck in real life.
takeaway: Load beside the live copy, then flip a pointer.
deeper:
**How a version swap works:** In general, the new version is written in full alongside the current one. Only when it is complete does serving switch to it, in one step. If the push fails, readers keep the old version.

**Why this fits derived data:** Derived datasets are recomputed wholesale by offline jobs, so replacing the whole thing is natural. Rolling back means switching to the previous version.

**The NameNode side:** HDFS keeps its namespace in one NameNode's memory. As files and blocks multiply, that single process becomes the limit. LinkedIn's clusters stored over 1 exabyte, with the largest around 10,000 nodes (2021), so keeping one NameNode healthy took sustained work.

**The contrast:** Google and Meta escaped the same limit by moving metadata into sharded stores: Colossus into Bigtable, Tectonic into ZippyDB. LinkedIn scaled HDFS vertically and horizontally instead.

quiz.q: A nightly job refreshes a 2 TB feature table in place, and users see mixed old and new scores for an hour. How would Venice change that?
quiz.a: Push the refreshed data as a complete new version beside the old one, then swap versions atomically. Readers see only the whole old or whole new dataset, never a mix.

mcq.q: What bottleneck did LinkedIn's 2021 HDFS post describe?
options: Keeping one NameNode healthy at huge object counts
DataNode disks filling faster than planned
Kafka lag between data centers
Venice version swaps taking too long
mcq.why: LinkedIn described heavy work to keep a single NameNode healthy at very large object counts, the HDFS metadata bottleneck.

hook: LinkedIn's first key-value store served read-only data from batch jobs. What did its replacement add?
title: Voldemort gave way to Venice; Hive gave way to Iceberg
body: Batch-only serving means data is only as fresh as the last push. LinkedIn's early Voldemort, a Dynamo-style key-value store from about 2009, served read-only data from batch jobs. **Venice** replaced that use case and added streaming, or **hybrid**, writes on top of batch pushes, so datasets can update between pushes. In the lake, LinkedIn has moved toward Iceberg tables with a control plane called **OpenHouse** (announced 2024), so table policies like retention are managed centrally.
takeaway: Replace a system when the new one can do what the old never could.
deeper:
**Why hybrid writes matter:** A pure batch store refreshes only when an offline job finishes. Streaming writes let fresh changes land between pushes, while batch pushes still rebuild the whole dataset.

**What stayed the same:** Venice keeps the push-based model: offline jobs push whole versions and Venice swaps them atomically. The upgrade added a capability rather than discarding the model.

**Why a control plane:** With many teams creating tables, policies like retention are hard to keep consistent if each team manages its own. OpenHouse manages them centrally.

**Why Iceberg:** Netflix created Iceberg because the older Hive layout on object storage had slow listing and no safe concurrent writes, and Iceberg tables can change partitioning without rewriting data.

**The pattern:** Both moves added what the old setup lacked: fresher data in Venice, central table policy in the lake.

quiz.q: A read-only store gets fresh data only from a nightly batch push, but product wants updates within minutes. What did LinkedIn's move to Venice add for this?
quiz.a: Streaming, or hybrid, writes on top of batch pushes, so changes land between nightly rebuilds while the batch push still refreshes the whole dataset.

mcq.q: What does OpenHouse do for LinkedIn's Iceberg lake?
options: Manages table policies like retention centrally
Replaces HDFS as the storage layer
Serves derived data to applications
Streams writes into Venice
mcq.why: OpenHouse, announced in 2024, is a control plane so Iceberg table policies such as retention are managed centrally.

hook: Dropbox stores exabytes of files as small blocks. How does it know where each block lives?
title: Magic Pocket: 4 MB blocks, named by their SHA-256 hash
body: File storage at Dropbox's scale needs a simple way to find and repair billions of pieces. **Magic Pocket**, public in 2016, is Dropbox's own block storage for file contents. Files split into blocks of up to 4 MB, each identified by its **SHA-256** hash. Blocks are grouped into 1 GB buckets, and cells hold about 50 PB raw. A sharded MySQL **Block Index** maps hashes to locations. Repair starts after a storage node has been offline for 15 minutes.
takeaway: Name data by its content, and much of the bookkeeping goes away.
deeper:
**Why hash-named blocks:** A block's name comes from its content, so identical blocks get identical names and a changed block gets a new one. Blocks never change in place, which keeps replication and repair simple.

**Why buckets:** Tracking billions of 4 MB blocks one at a time is heavy. Grouping them into 1 GB buckets lets placement and repair work on bigger units.

**Why wait 15 minutes:** Many node outages are brief, like a reboot. Waiting avoids copying terabytes for a node that comes right back, while still starting repair promptly.

**Keep it simple:** A central master per cell, no distributed consensus in the data path, and a very small team.

**The scale:** Cells of about 50 PB raw, multiple exabytes in total (2016).

quiz.q: Two users upload the same 4 MB chunk of a file. What does Magic Pocket's content addressing imply for how that block is named and found?
quiz.a: Both chunks hash to the same SHA-256 value, so they share one block name, and the Block Index maps that hash to one set of locations.

mcq.q: What maps block hashes to storage locations in Magic Pocket?
options: A sharded MySQL Block Index
A Paxos-replicated metadata service
Each storage node's local directory
Amazon S3 object keys
mcq.why: A sharded MySQL Block Index maps each block's SHA-256 hash to where the block lives.

predict.q: How long does Magic Pocket wait after a storage node goes offline before starting repair?
options: 15 minutes
15 seconds
24 hours

hook: Dropbox moved most of its users' files off Amazon S3 in about 14 months. What came first?
title: Dropbox left S3 with a dark launch, then a slow cutover
body: Cutting over a storage backend in one move bets every file on day one. Dropbox didn't. It **dark-launched** Magic Pocket in August 2014, running it alongside S3. From February 2015, new files were stored only in-house. By October 2015, over 90 percent of user data had moved off Amazon S3. The reasons: end-to-end control of performance and better **unit economics** at Dropbox's scale.
takeaway: Mirror for months, then cut over. Confidence is earned in the shadows.
deeper:
**What a dark launch buys:** The new system handles real traffic before anyone depends on it. Bugs, performance gaps and data mismatches show up while S3 still serves users.

**Why new files first:** Once new writes go only in-house, the old system stops growing. Existing data can then move in the background at a controlled pace.

**The timeline:**
1. August 2014: dark launch.
2. February 2015: new files stored only in-house.
3. October 2015: over 90 percent of user data off S3.

**Why it paid for Dropbox:** File storage is its product, storage dominates its cost, and the workload is simple immutable blocks. Owning the stack pays under those conditions.

**Not a full exit:** Dropbox still uses AWS where it makes sense, especially outside the US.

quiz.q: You're replacing your blob store. A teammate wants to copy all data over one weekend and switch reads on Monday. What would Dropbox's sequence suggest instead?
quiz.a: Dark-launch the new store beside the old one, send new writes to it once it proves out, then migrate existing data gradually, keeping the old store as a fallback.

mcq.q: What was the first step of Dropbox's move off S3?
options: A dark launch of Magic Pocket in August 2014
Deleting all data from S3 in February 2015
Moving only non-US users in 2014
Rewriting clients to a new API first
mcq.why: Dropbox dark-launched Magic Pocket in August 2014, stored new files only in-house from February 2015, and moved 90%+ by October 2015.

hook: Dropbox's move off S3 paid off. Why would the same move likely lose money for most companies?
title: Owning storage pays only when storage is your big cost
body: Dropbox is the classic case where buy then build paid off. It started on Amazon S3, then built Magic Pocket. Two conditions made it work. Storage was most of its cost, so the savings were large. And its **workload was simple**: immutable, content-addressed blocks. When storage is most of your cost and your workload is simple, owning the stack pays. When storage is a small part of your cost, it rarely does, because you lack the scale to amortize a **storage team**.
takeaway: Build storage when its bill is your business. Otherwise, rent.
deeper:
**The second axis:** How large is your storage bill as a share of total cost? When storage dominates cost, as at Dropbox or Meta for photos, owning the hardware and the erasure codes pays for a team. When it does not, as at most product companies, buying wins.

**Why simplicity matters:** Immutable blocks named by hash are among the easiest data to store at scale: no updates in place, easy repair, easy verification. That let a very small team run exabytes with a central master per cell and no distributed consensus in the data path.

**The hidden cost of building:** Hardware, data centers, on-call, repair tooling and years of hardening. At small scale that cost is spread over too few bytes.

**Not all-or-nothing:** Dropbox still uses AWS where it makes sense, especially outside the US.

**Ask this:** If our storage bill went to zero, would the business look different?

quiz.q: A B2B SaaS company spends 4% of its costs on storage and asks whether to leave S3 as Dropbox did. What do you say?
quiz.a: Probably not. Storage is a small share of its cost, so the savings can't fund a storage team at its scale. Dropbox paid off because storage dominated its cost and the workload was simple.

mcq.q: Which pair of conditions made Dropbox's buy-then-build pay off?
options: Storage was most of its cost; the workload was simple blocks
It had many teams; each needed its own database
It sold cloud services; it ran many regions
Its data was mutable; it needed strong consistency
mcq.why: Owning pays when storage dominates cost and the workload is simple, like Dropbox's immutable, content-addressed blocks.

hook: Apple's CloudKit gives every user a separate database for every app. How many databases is that?
title: CloudKit runs billions of tiny databases on FoundationDB
body: Giving each user of each app its own database sounds impossible to operate. Apple does it with key prefixes. It acquired **FoundationDB** in 2015 and open-sourced it in 2018. The Record Layer paper (2019) says CloudKit uses the **Record Layer** on FoundationDB to host billions of independent logical databases, one per user per app, serving hundreds of millions of users. Each tiny database is a key-prefix range inside a shared FoundationDB cluster.
takeaway: A tenant can be a key prefix, not a server.
deeper:
**How a database becomes a prefix:** FoundationDB is an ordered key-value store. Put every key for one user's app data under the same prefix, and that range behaves like its own database. Creating a tenant means using a new prefix.

**The architecture:** A single strongly consistent, ordered, transactional key-value core, with thin stateless layers on top that add records, indexes and queries. The Record Layer is one such layer.

**Why stateless layers:** State lives only in FoundationDB, so layer servers can be added or replaced freely. Transactions in the core keep a record and its indexes consistent.

**Multi-tenancy at the extreme:** Billions of logical databases share one cluster instead of billions of servers or files.

**What else Apple published:** Advanced Data Protection (2022) lets users end-to-end encrypt most iCloud data.

quiz.q: You're building a SaaS product with a million small customers, each wanting isolated data. How would Apple's CloudKit pattern structure it?
quiz.a: Keep all tenants in one ordered, transactional key-value cluster, give each tenant its own key prefix, and put stateless layers for records, indexes and queries on top.

mcq.q: In CloudKit, what is each per-user, per-app database physically?
options: A key-prefix range in a shared FoundationDB cluster
A separate FoundationDB cluster per user
A SQLite file on a dedicated server
A bucket in an object store
mcq.why: The Record Layer hosts billions of logical databases, each a key-prefix range inside a shared FoundationDB cluster.

predict.q: Per the 2019 Record Layer paper, how many logical databases does CloudKit host on FoundationDB?
options: Billions
Millions
Thousands

hook: iCloud users can turn on one setting that locks Apple out of their data. What does it change on Apple's side?
title: With Advanced Data Protection, Apple holds no keys
body: Encryption at rest protects disks, but the provider's servers can still decrypt your data. **Advanced Data Protection**, introduced in 2022, lets users turn on **end-to-end encryption** for most iCloud data categories, so Apple does not hold the keys. Apple's servers still store the data, but only as ciphertext they cannot read. Anything that needs the plaintext has to happen on the user's own devices, which hold the keys.
takeaway: Whoever holds the key decides what the server can do.
deeper:
**At rest vs end-to-end:** With encryption at rest, as at S3, Azure and Google Cloud by default, the provider's servers can still use keys to decrypt and process data. With end-to-end encryption, keys live only on the user's devices.

**What the server loses:** Server-side features that read content, like search or indexing, stop working on that data. Meta hit the same limit when Messenger made end-to-end encryption the default in December 2023.

**What the user takes on:** In general, end-to-end systems shift key custody, and its risks, to the user. A provider without keys cannot decrypt data for someone who lost theirs.

**Why "most" categories:** ADP covers most iCloud data categories, not all of them.

**Design question:** For each feature, does it need the server to read content? If yes, it conflicts with end-to-end encryption.

quiz.q: A company already encrypts all customer data at rest with keys it manages. Why is that not the same as Apple's Advanced Data Protection?
quiz.a: With encryption at rest, the provider's servers can still use keys to decrypt and process data. ADP is end-to-end: Apple doesn't hold the keys, so its servers see only ciphertext.

mcq.q: What changes when an iCloud user enables Advanced Data Protection?
options: Apple no longer holds the keys for most iCloud data
Apple keeps the data in one region only
Apple stops storing the data on its servers
Apple switches the data to customer KMS keys
mcq.why: ADP turns on end-to-end encryption for most iCloud categories, so Apple doesn't hold the keys; it still stores the ciphertext.

hook: Pinterest's graph service ran on HBase for years, and its data kept drifting out of sync. What was causing it?
title: Pinterest moved its graph from HBase to TiDB
body: Pinterest runs on AWS and historically used HBase heavily. Its graph service, Zen, was built on HBase and MySQL in 2014. It later moved to **TiDB**, a distributed SQL database, as **PinGraph**. The reasons: data inconsistencies from application-level secondary indexes, limited query patterns, and a 10-year-old codebase. The case study reports 1.5 PB, 8 million QPS at peak, over 100 use cases and over 50 percent lower infrastructure cost.

stat.label: up to 10× lower P99 latency on TiDB

takeaway: When the database can't keep index and data together, change databases.
deeper:
**Why app-level indexes drift:** Without transactions, the application writes the data and then the index as two separate operations. A crash between them leaves one without the other, and nothing repairs it.

**What TiDB brought:** Native transactions, so data and index update together, plus SQL for richer query patterns than Zen supported.

**The results, per the case study:**
1. 1.5 PB of data and 8 million QPS at peak.
2. Over 100 use cases.
3. Up to 10× lower P99 latency.
4. Over 50 percent lower infrastructure cost.

**Caveat:** These figures come from PingCAP's case study, a vendor source, dated only to the 2020s. Read them as reported, not independently measured.
